stories.body:
Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts

Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.

Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.

In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”

Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.

Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.

The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.

Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.

“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”

Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.

“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.

In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.

Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.

Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

stories.title: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid: Drives like an EV, but there's no plug involved
stories.summary: Nissan’s series hybrid e-Power system has been retuned for American roads.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Nissan’s series hybrid e-Power system has been retuned for American roads.

Nissan has a new version of its best-selling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested back in February. Most of the hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid.

That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V . Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars’ gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiast irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for.

Series hybrids

Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher.

This charges a 1.67 kWh lithium-ion traction battery that has been optimized for its charge and discharge ability, which in turn powers a pair of electric motors. At the front axle sits a 202 hp (150 kW), 243 lb-ft (330 Nm) permanent synchronous magnet motor, at the rear another PSM providing 134 hp (100 kW) and 144 lb-ft (195 Nm), although given the battery’s limitations, combined power output is 225 hp (168 kW). And as you would expect, the motors will regeneratively brake under deceleration to return as much energy to the battery for reuse as possible.

Although this is the first time Nissan has offered the e-Power hybrid system here in the US, it has been on sale in Japan for a decade now, with more than 1.4 million cars on the road in that time. Those versions weren’t considered quite sufficient for our roads, so Nissan retuned the system for the Rogue Hybrid to be able to cope with harder acceleration and bigger vehicles.

Enjoyable to drive

From behind the wheel, you could very easily forget this wasn’t just a new EV—a replacement for the gone-too-soon Ariya, perhaps. Throttle tip-in is immediate, like any good electric car, and there’s enough torque to get you on your way without any fuss, even if a 0–60 mph (97 km/h) time of 6.4 seconds isn’t particularly fast by 2026 standards. Nissan has had plenty of expertise in calibrating one-pedal driving setups, and when you access the Rogue Hybrid’s by pushing a button on the center console, you’ll find it’s no different here.

So keen was Nissan to demonstrate the smoothness with which the powertrain decelerates under regen braking that it put us through a mini school-run obstacle course, complete with a fishbowl full of water mounted to the cupholder. Nary a drop was spilled, versus the same test in what might be the Rogue Hybrid’s greatest rival, Toyota’s hybrid RAV4 . (The RAV4, with no one-pedal driving, requires you to use the brake pedal to slow and stop.)

Acceleration is good at highway speeds, and cruising is quiet—on a wet and windy day it was the gusts we heard, rather than wind noise generated by the car. Speaking of generators, you don’t really hear the engine running much either. It never revs particularly high and shuts off whenever possible—with music playing on the infotainment system, the occupants might not even notice.

The ride absorbed bumps on the road well, but it didn’t absorb sharp transient shocks as well as it did those of longer duration. A combination of low-rolling resistance tires and Californian roads that were seeing their first rain in some time conspired to create rather a lot of understeer as I entered a roundabout with perhaps a touch more vigor than normal. That said, I rather liked the Rogue Hybrid’s steering feel, and together with the smooth power delivery from the two electric motors and the easy one-pedal driving mode, my time behind the wheel was most pleasant.

To live with?

The Rogue Hybrid SR we drove is rated at 41 mpg (5.7 L/100 km) in the city, 36 mpg (6.5 L/100 km) highway, and a combined 38 mpg (6.2 L/100 km), not quite as good as the RAV4 hybrid but still competitive with the segment.

The Rogue Hybrid provided a commendable amount of storage space, and I was glad to see so many physical controls. As our car was fitted with the Tech package, it included a larger 14.3-inch touchscreen infotainment system running Android Automotive OS with google automotive services. Wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay are available with both this and the standard 12.3-inch system, and I was surprised to discover that the Rogue Hybrid would show Google Maps navigation from an iPhone through CarPlay on the main instrument display in front of the driver—usually only Apple Maps (and Waze iirc) appear on this screen, with Google Maps relegated to the infotainment display.

Seat comfort has long been a Nissan obsession, and its work on its “Zero Gravity” seats has paid off, as a day of driving did not result in a fatigued driver. The stitching and design of the seats was inspired by cozy puffer jackets, although I think the charcoal interior would be a better idea for life with a family or animals than the light gray of our test car.

Initially, Nissan will just have a single flavor of Rogue Hybrid for sale, the SR with the Tech Package, which will cost $41,490. In January, it will add the $35,490 SV and the $43,490 Platinum trims to the mix, prices that are benchmarked against the aforementioned Toyota. And for those who think you’ll only be able to find the most expensive ones at the dealership, Nissan says it expects the mix to be 30 percent SV, 50 percent SR, 20 percent Platinum.

Honest question: what is the ultimate benefit of these hybrids? They burn slightly less fossils, but can also burn the same or more, depending how they are driven. And have much higher complexity than a pure BEV or petrol.

stories.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost concerns
stories.summary: Shares in Intel have continued to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 30 October 2026, 14:50 GMT

US stocks have continued to slide as concerns continue to intensify over the increasing costs of the artificial intelligence (AI) build out.

Shares in Intel continued their overnight slide into early trading on Friday, falling as much as 30% after the chip maker warned of a weaker computer market even as it plans to increase spending on AI.

Amazon shares fell as far as 6% before recovering after its reported earnings on Thursday evening fell short of investors' expectations.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange opened on Friday at its lowest level in more than two months, down 2.5%, as other tech stocks including Reddit and Roblox continued to fall.

The losses follow the value of Google owner Alphabet plunging by more than $500bn on Thursday after it revealed its own AI summaries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.

Alphabet stock continued to fall in early trading, down 1% after Thursday's massive slide.

The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere, with Intel on track to lose more than $130bn in value after its earnings update rattled investors.

On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect positive cash flow this year, and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.

"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.

In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.

stories.body:
Will staking everything on AI work?

Perspectiverox asks : The government has an enormous amount riding on AI to deliver future economic growth. Do you think this strategy will work? And is the government’s heavy investment in this vision, and its apparent determination to pursue it, contributing to a failure to properly acknowledge or address serious public concerns about the environment and jobs? More fundamentally, what happens if the anticipated AI-driven growth doesn’t materialise? Is there a Plan B?

double quotation mark Aditya says: In their book When Nothing Works, the Foundational Economy collective of economists and analysts point out that after decades of successive governments in the UK talking up the ‘knowledge economy’, technology accounted for less than 5% of GDP. That wasn’t just a British failure – the story is same across much of Europe. This is before we get intot who benefits from AI. I find the slavering of the UK’s politicians and press before America’s AI oligarchy vulgar and idiotic, especially when all the indications are that these trade deals work against the interest of Britons. The other clear thing is that AI hyperscalers and Trump are forcing Americans through a bubble. When it pops it will be a political failure, a market failure, an economic failure. Your question about Plan B is interesting. What does the Left do when the AI Bubbles pops? I think my first ever column for the Guardian was in August 2008, before the collapse of Lehman Brothers , where I said the Left should get ready for a looming crisis (Call me Mystic Meg, why not). The former editor of the Economist, Bill Emmott, told me I was a silly boy and this would all blow over . Never waste a good crisis.

How do we rid ourselves of neoliberalist thinking?

Odourcolon asks : Do you think it’s possible to get rid of the neoliberalist thought process that seems to have dominated, and ruined (?), the UK over the past few decades?

Doodah70 asks : Aditya, what does getting rid of neo liberalism actually mean? It seems to be a narrative of taking us back to the economic policies of the 1970s and has a rose tinted view of that period ignoring inflation, IMF bailouts and mass industrial unrest and strike action. Is there an example of a country that doesn’t follow neoliberal ideas, that is successful, that we can emulate?

double quotation mark Aditya says: Hello both, these are very good questions. I rarely use the term neoliberal in my own writing. Partly because I am not sure enough readers will have a clear sense of what it means, as Doodah says, and partly because when I am talking about neoliberalism I might be referring to: 1) handing public assets to private actors 2) reducing the active role of the state in providing essentials 3) weakening the power of labour 4) the bulldozing of institutions such as trade unions and the BBC And on and on Some of these processes are well described by the political economist Will Davies when he describes the ideology of neoliberalism as “the disenchantment of politics by economics”. The reality is that few countries have gone as far down the same path as the UK: the first country to industrialise and the first rich country really to de-industrialise. The first social democratic polity to privatise at this scale. Filleting the BBC, an institution which so many other countries envy Not all of this can be reversed, at least by much. I can’t see a quick path back to major manufacturing status – not now we’ve destroyed our supply chains. After starting on his March of the Makers, George Osborne did not make it far. (For a different view of this problem, look at Reindustrialise Britain, by Costas Lapavitsas, my dear former colleague Larry Elliott and Doug Nicholls). But other avenues look more promising. Look at what Angela Rayner has begun with employment rights and renters rights – many in politics know some of the problems, it’s just that their solutions are too bitty.

Are public schools justified?

John Buckler asks : Please, can you justify for me private education in our society when it sucks up our scant resources to over-educate the mediocre, elevating them to positions of power eg Mogg, Gove, Johnson, Farage ?

double quotation mark Aditiya says: Thank you for your kind invitation, John, but I must decline.

Why Michael Gove?

George Fidler asks : On your podcast Radical Thinking why did you interview Michael Gove – someone whose politics are as orthodox as they can be in Britain? A similar thing happened with Rayner’s Beyond the Bubble. You would be hard pressed to find someone more central to the bubble than Gove. Genuinely, I don’t think there’s anything “radical” that can be learned from him. A second and related question. Would you consider interviewing Andreas Malm?

double quotation mark Aditya says: Thanks for listening, George. Your question is the one with which I start that interview : why is something called Radical Thinking spending time with Michael Gove? The answer comes in two parts: One, across the West (and elsewhere) the radical politics that is taking the lead is not from the Left, but the Right. Think of Nigel Farage in the UK, Alice Weidel of the AfD, Giorgia Maloni running Italy, her past in neo-fascist politics. And two: Gove is a thinker, an intelligent man who has both led the Right (one of the fathers of Brexit, don’t forget) and followed it (think of what he publishes as the editor today of the Spectator). FWIW, I found that interview fascinating. Here was a man accepting that the Conservatism that he’d previously championed was dead, and that its successor was a new, nastier, nativist right that derived much of its legitimacy from the failures of him and his colleagues. Think about living with that knowledge.

Where is the outrage over inequality?

redstar1000 asks : Britain has some of the highest levels of deprivation in Europe. Millions of people in one of the richest countries in the world cannot eat well, keep their homes warm and take part in social life. Why is this seen as acceptable? Where is the moral outrage?

double quotation mark Aditya says: This is a great question that chimes with the one above. I share your outrage and so do others. Confronted with the situation you describe - around 300,000 households in England homeless , many of them with children - in one of the richest societies in human history, they would agree this is unacceptable, outrageous. But in a highly-unequal country, not everyone sees or feels or even brushes against this deprivation.

Are we heading for total economic and social collapse?

Flaxborough asks : Hi Aditya, can you answer truthfully, do you think we are heading for total economic and social collapse? How soon? Will we rise from it afterwards?

double quotation mark Aditya says: In truth, I think the UK is in economic and social collapse – it’s just that some people can’t see it, and others are too polite or arrogant to point it out. But what else should we call the most miserable period for wages and growth since Napoleon Bonaparte was on his horse charging around Europe? The worst decade for living standards since the end of rationing? Shit in our rivers? Joke prime ministers who blunder about, get booted offstage, then earn £££s? And no, not just Liz Truss, but Cameron and Johnson too. The reason this isn’t recognised is because Britain is a highly unequal country where pain is heaped on those most hurt. Even in a collapsing country, some people always do well. Look at Argentina in the 1990s/2000s for an example. Flaxborough, my friend, don’t ask when collapse will arrive: recognise it’s here already. And push for something better.

Radical thinking - or politics?

Michael Holmes asks: I have enjoyed all the talks. I am just a bit confused that the title of the talk varies between ‘Radical thinking’ and ‘Politics’, are they different categories? They seem to have the same production team. Also, the earlier programming had suggestions by you for further reading. This now doesn’t seem to happen? I thought that was valuable. I really enjoy the thoughtful interaction between you and your guests, with the time allowed for thoughtful and creative content. Great stuff! Thanks

double quotation mark Aditya says: Thanks so much for this, Michael. It’s great to get your feedback on the Radical Thinking podcast – and I’d love to hear more from viewers and listeners about what they are enjoying from the series so far. Just to explain: Radical Thinking began as a one-off series of conversations. The idea was to capture some of the energy and ideas of this particular moment – a change of prime minister in the UK, Trump and the midterms, the rise of the far right. We publish every weekend here as well as YouTube, Spotify, Apple. This Saturday’s episode is with two of the best dissenting economists around on some of the central issues in this week’s Budget – it’s a corker. You’re right – part of our (tiny) team is from Politics Weekly and because it’s a one-off we don’t have a separate channel. HOWEVER! The reaction so far has been astonishing, so strong that we’re thinking about more. So: watch this space Glad you like the further reading. Again, I started it as an experiment – and I know it hasn’t appeared everywhere – but if it’s useful i’ll keep it up.

Welcome to the Conversation

Aditya Chakrabortty is the Guardian’s award-winning senior economics commentator. Through his regular opinion column, he shares his thoughts on the economy and its impact on society and earlier this year he was awarded an MBE for services to public understanding of the economy and wider social issues.

This month he launched a new Saturday podcast Radical Thinking, where he interviews major thinkers about the ideas that have shaped our times. He has conducted conversations with Yanis Varoufakis on democracy and the Eurozone crisis and Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor on Gaza, fascism and climate chaos.

In his latest episode he discusses doomscrolling and democracy with playwright James Graham who suggests that our algorithms have led us into ‘a massive crisis of the new’ and are preventing us from imagining a different future.

Aditya will be online at 2pm GMT (9am EDT) today to answer your questions on economics, democracy, the future of British and global politics.

stories.title: Winter fuel cuts turned the Welsh against Labour, former leader Neil Kinnock says
stories.summary: The former Labour leader says welfare policies turned disillusionment with Labour into "active dislike".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lord Kinnock says UK Labour decisions led to "dislike" of the Welsh arm of the party

Published 1 hour ago

Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock says the party's welfare policies turned disillusionment with Labour in Wales into "active dislike".

He said that UK government decisions on benefits and winter fuel payments had driven voters in Wales away from the Welsh arm of the party before the country's Senedd election in May.

Lord Kinnock made the comments as part of a Newyddion S4C YouTube special on Andy Burnham's first 100 days as Prime Minister.

Governing "at both ends of the M4" before Wales' parliamentary elections had presented an extra challenge for his party, he said.

Winter fuel payments fell by 9.3 million before U-turn Published 16 September 2025

He said: "If there is any opposition or resentment to the government on either end of the M4, the other lot are going to pay as well."

"There is no doubt in my mind," he said, that "alienation... had been creeping up."

"It could be a mixture of boredom. It could be a mixture of dislike," Kinnock said.

He said "what turned that into active dislike" had been things "like the withdrawal of the winter fuel allowance, the threats to the welfare system" and not scrapping a cap on two child benefits quick enough.

In June last year, the Labour UK government U-turned on its controversial decision to means-test winter fuel payments for pensioners in England and Wales.

Almost one year later, Labour lost power in Wales in a seismic election in May, returning just nine Senedd members after running the Welsh government for 27 years.

Lord Kinnock, who is the father of Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock, also said he reservations about devolving justice to Wales - a key demand of the Plaid Cymru Welsh government.

Plaid ministers say it would allow for a more effective system tailored to Welsh communities and better integrated with health, housing and education.

Kinnock said there would no be "much of an argument" against the idea if it meant that "Wales was better protected, that the streets were safer" and "that the justice system was more efficient".

"But those guarantees are absent at the moment," he said.

"Until they exist, until they're in place, the upheaval of creating what would have to be effectively a new system with new management... with an introverted view of the justice system - there would be more downsides than upsides."

"Now that picture might change, but as I can see it now in October 2026, that's where we are, there are more disadvantages than advantages."

stories.title: Trump declares robot imports a national security threat
stories.summary: President orders trade talks on foreign-made factory robots, threatens tariffs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
President orders trade talks on foreign-made factory robots, threatens tariffs.

President Donald Trump has declared the imports of foreign-made factory robots to be a national security threat—ordering new US negotiations with trading partners while holding out the possibility of imposing new tariffs on such robot imports in the future.

Issued on October 28, Trump’s presidential proclamation represents heightened government scrutiny of foreign-made industrial robots that could complicate the manufacturing operations of major US corporations that rely on such robots. Those companies include Detroit automakers General Motors and Ford, electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla , and aerospace and defense giants like Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Trump’s proclamation describes industrial robots and machinery as being crucial for producing US military weapon systems along with representing a “driving force” behind all critical infrastructure sectors within the US economy. The proclamation cites an investigation under US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick as having found that US imports of such robots “pose[] risks to the United States industrial base and threatens the long-term competitiveness of the United States in a sector that is increasingly vital to national security.”

The Department of Commerce investigation also supposedly found “unique security and safety risks” that may introduce “significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities that can result in severe consequences to the United States.”

Such wording echoes justifications used by Trump’s Federal Communications Commission when it banned new models of foreign-made robots, such as robotic vacuums, four-legged robot dogs, and humanoid robots, in July 2026. But that FCC action had specifically exempted industrial robot arms and other fixed or stationary robots commonly deployed in automotive factories and logistics warehouses.

Now Trump’s directive for the United States and trading partners “to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components” aims to strike new agreements on the issue within 180 days of the proclamation’s date. If no agreements have been reached by then, the proclamation warns that the president may take additional actions, like imposing “tariffs, duties, quotas, and fees” on such imports.

Any tariffs or other fees would, of course, be paid by the US companies importing such foreign-made robots. That would likely increase the cost of US manufacturing operations at a time when the United States has become the second largest market in using industrial robots, with the International Federation of Robotics reporting nearly 38,500 new US installations of industrial robots in 2025.

Major US automotive and aerospace companies often buy large robotic arms for factory floor work from the “big four” robotics makers—FANUC, ABB, Yaskawa, and KUKA—that are headquartered in Japan, Switzerland, and Germany. No US company currently offers comparable heavy-duty hardware for large industrial robotic arms, although the foreign robotics makers have been expanding their US engineering and assembly facilities.

Even Amazon, the company that has arguably deployed more robot workers than any other in the world, still uses some foreign-made robots, like Japan’s FANUC robotic arms, despite having significantly ramped up its own in-house robot production and developed certain specialized robotic arms.

Trump’s own proclamation acknowledges that US robotics companies do not produce enough industrial robots to “meet national security needs,” and that the United States “relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery and for their components.”

If Trump eventually slaps tariffs on US imports of foreign-made industrial robots, that would at least fall short of restricting imports outright. Although as Intel recently showed, major US companies can still get waivers from the Trump administration to continue using foreign-made robots even when a nominal ban is in place.

stories.body:
‘Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them’

Donald Trump successfully campaigned for his second term two years ago promising to reduce prices on day one , but ever since he returned to the White House, he has done little to fight inflation or reduce prices. Instead, some of his most important policy decisions – most notably his war against Iran and his tariff wars – have increased inflation instead of reducing it. This helps explain why more than one in five Americans who voted for Trump now disapprove of the job he’s doing.

Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them during his second term. Indeed, the “ liberation day ” tariffs he imposed soon after returning to office increased the price of hundreds of goods, including citrus fruits , steel, bananas, beef and auto parts. When the supreme court overturned those tariffs as illegal, Trump immediately imposed new 10% across-the-board tariffs that again helped push up prices (a lower court found those tariffs unlawful, too ). Time and again, Trump has slapped on new tariffs even though they inherently push up prices because tariffs are a tax on imported goods. Little wonder that a Fox News poll this month found that 77% of Americans disapprove of how Trump has handled tariffs.

Candidate Trump pledged to slash “energy and electricity prices by half” , to get “gasoline below $2 a gallon” , and to bring down “airfares and housing costs”. He has failed to do any of those things. Gas now averages $4.28 a gallon nationally, according to AAA . Yale Budget Lab says Trump’s tariffs will cost the average household $1,100 this year, while Moody’s Analytics says the war with Iran has already cost US households about $2,000 from higher energy, fuel and transportation costs and from higher interest rates.

Worsening Americans’ affordability problems, prices have been rising faster than workers’ wages in recent months. As a result, Americans have seen no real wage growth on average since Trump returned to office – both average hourly pay and prices have risen by 5.4% since January 2025.

Matthew Middleton, a White House spokesman, defended Trump’s record on inflation and critiqued Joe Biden’s, saying: “President Trump has implemented an aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda that has blunted Biden’s historic 40-year high inflation crisis, driven economic growth, increased wages and created private-sector jobs in areas that had been hollowed out and shipped overseas.”

After returning to the White House, Trump helped push up electricity prices by ending federal subsidies for low-cost renewable energy . His gung-ho cheerleading for datacenters, along with his speeding up of federal permitting to build them , has helped fuel a datacenter construction boom that is expected to increase electricity costs to consumers by more than $6bn . Trump and the Republican-led Congress further hit consumers by raising the cost of many electric vehicles by $7,500 when they ended EV subsidies.

When Trump plunged into war against Iran eight months ago, he showed little concern about what that war would mean for inflation back home. He ignored warnings that the war would cause Iran to close the strait of Hormuz , which in turn would cause oil and gas prices to soar. Since the war began, US gas prices have risen by over 40%, diesel prices by nearly 70%, and some fertilizer prices by 20% . Record diesel prices have pushed airfares skyward, while soaring diesel and fertilizer prices have created a sea of red ink for US farmers.

In one tiff over inflation, after Trump said last June “ I love the inflation ,” Senator Bernie Sanders responded , “You know who doesn’t love inflation, Mr President? Working families struggling to afford gas, groceries and other necessities because of your disastrous actions.”

Further defending Trump’s record on inflation, White House spokesman Middleton said: “The President has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but this administration will continue to deliver economic wins for the American people over the next two years. While Democrats pretend to care about ‘affordability’, this administration has delivered tangible wins to make life more affordable for American families: President Trump signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals and will continue to put American workers first.”

A White House official added that Trump’s policies “have created an environment for sustained increase in energy supply and lower costs for American households and businesses”. Those policies have included making it easier to drill for oil and reducing business and environmental regulations.

Trump’s moves have further worsened Americans’ affordability woes by pushing up interest rates. By the time Biden left office, inflation, which had soared to a painful 9% during the pandemic, had slid to 3.0% and was heading lower. But Trump’s policies have played a major role in pushing inflation back up to 3.7% . That has caused the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, while also pushing mortgage rates higher. Thirty-year fixed mortgage rates have climbed to 7.4%, making it considerably harder for young and non-affluent Americans to buy homes. (As for Trump’s 2024 promise to reduce housing costs, he refused to sign a bipartisan bill that sought to speed housing construction with the aim of making housing more affordable.)

Under Trump, not only has the national debt climbed above $40tn, but this year’s federal budget deficit will reach $2tn. That worsening fiscal picture has worried bond investors and pushed up interest rates. (In 2019, Trump promised to eliminate the entire national debt within eight years.)

Trump’s policies have increased healthcare costs for millions of Americans. By pushing Congress to cut Medicaid by $1tn and to not extend Obamacare subsidies, Trump helped cause more than 20 million people to lose health coverage or pay more out-of-pocket for healthcare. Americans who pay for their own health insurance saw their premiums jump by 25% this year , with many households paying not just hundreds of dollars more, but thousands more.

To be sure, Trump has taken several steps to fight inflation, but most have been minor. His TrumpRX program has offered many drugs at lower prices, and that was one factor among many that contributed to the 4.5% drop in prescription drug prices over the past year. In August, Trump announced he would import 660m pounds of ground beef from Latin America to reduce beef prices – that move (which angered ranchers) was a direct response to the public outcry over the higher beef prices resulting from his tariffs. Last November, in a sharp about-face aimed at reducing prices, Trump rescinded his tariffs on coffee and tropical fruits after consumers had grown angry that coffee and citrus prices had soared due to Trump’s tariffs.

With his promise to pay $5,000 to every adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, Trump is essentially saying he will make it up to voters for pushing up prices and worsening affordability problems. Trump says the money for those payments could come from tariff revenues , but guess where those tariffs revenues come from? They come from the money that US consumers have had to pay on Trump’s tariffs – on his taxes on imports. Some might say that Trump wants to pay Peter by first robbing Peter.

Trump keeps saying that affordability problems are “a hoax” . But whenever average Americans go to a supermarket or gas station, they know that the affordability squeeze is real and a big issue in their lives. Many can see that Trump, despite his campaign promises, has done precious little to reduce inflation. Indeed, in very bad news for Republicans in the midterm elections, a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 78% of Americans blame Trump’s policies for pushing up prices.

The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping

China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.

A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.

Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.

The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.

“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.

The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.

Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.

A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.

Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.

The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong.

The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

Newquay Mayor Drew Creek said he could not stand by the Greens' Zionism is racism motion

Published 1 hour ago

The leader of the Green Party on Cornwall Council has defected following the party's recent "Zionism is racism" motion.

Drew Creek joined the Labour and Co-operatives on Thursday after the policy motion was passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.

Creek, who is Mayor of Newquay and serves as a councillor for Trenance ward, said he had "huge respect" for Greens across Cornwall but the motion "crossed a line".

The Cornwall Green Party said it was "deeply saddened" by Creek's decision to join Labour and said it does not "try to impose uniformity of belief" among its members and elected representatives.

More news stories for Cornwall

Listen to the latest news for Cornwall

The motion backed by Green members at its party conference said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It has been criticised by Jewish groups , as well as some Green MPs and opposition political parties .

Creek said he hoped the Green Party would step back from the stance – but said instead, "Zack Polanski and the leadership has doubled down".

"I can't stand behind that, and I won't pretend otherwise," the councillor said.

He added: "People in Newquay don't want politicians driving division. They want someone who'll fix the roads, protect our coast, fight for local services and bring people together.

"That's the kind of politics I believe in and the kind of politics Andy Burnham has shown.

Zack Polanski previously said he would not overturn the motion

"Newquay is my home and where I am raising my family. I came into politics for one reason, to stand up for this town and the people in it. Labour is where I believe I can do that best, and I'm looking forward to getting on with the job."

Councillor Kate Ewert, Labour and Co-operative Group Leader on Cornwall Council said Creek's decision "highlights the serious questions about Zack Polanski's leadership".

Noah Law, MP for St Austell and Newquay, added: "In this period of polarised politics, it takes great courage to stand up for what you believe in.

"Having worked with Drew since my election, I have always found him to be steadfast in his beliefs, easy to work with, and a good advocate for Newquay."

'Disagreements'

A spokesperson for the Cornwall Green Party said Creek had "done excellent work as a Green councillor" and they understood there were "different views within the Green Party on the 'Zionism is Racism' motion".

They said: "Disagreements over the wording of this one motion should not distract from the fact that the Green Party is united in its condemnation of the racist genocide and ethnic cleansing that Israel is perpetrating in Gaza and the occupied territories, and united in its demand for much tougher sanctions on Israel.

"Labour, by contrast, refuses even to recognise that what we are seeing is genocide, and continues to allow arms exports to and intelligence-sharing with the government that is committing it.

"It's hard to see how anyone who is serious about action on climate, action to end extreme inequality, and action to prevent an ongoing genocide could switch their support to a party that is not serious about any of these."

stories.summary: In today’s digital world, the internet is an essential resource for young people to access information, explore community, and find themselves. But we know that this often comes alongside fears of experiencing online harms like doxxing, grooming, or bullying. Trying to protect your family from everything all the time is impractical and exhausting, but some thoughtful planning can help families devise a workable plan that meets their needs and addresses their concerns. That’s why this Digital Parent Week, we’re sharing easy tips on how parents and their children can work together to co-curate a digital safety plan that helps all members of the family enjoy the benefits of technology while protecting their online privacy and safety. Start with Open Conversations Online safety begins with communication, not just restrictions. Talk with a young person about how they use the internet: their favourite apps, games, and social media platforms for example. How bad are the consequences if we fail? e.g, losing some money on a scam or having creepy conversations with strangers that could escalate into something more nefarious or dangerous. stories.title: Victory! You Can Now Exclude Apps from Siri AI
stories.summary: In the most recent update to Apple’s devices, iOS 27.2, the company has introduced a new setting to “Exclude Apps” from Siri AI, fulfilling one of our asks from our Encrypt It Already campaign earlier this year . One of our main concerns with new AI features on devices is how those features interact with end-to-end encrypted content, particularly with secure messaging apps. Many AI features require cloud processing, and despite privacy protections engineered into these systems , the content of secure messaging apps may leave a user’s device without their knowledge. That changes the privacy concerns around using those tools. In a perfect world, users would be able to put a barrier up to ensure data from certain apps doesn’t leave the device. Here was our initial ask: You should be able to tell the operating system’s AI to not access an app, even if that comes at the “cost” of missing out on some features. The setting should be straightforward and easy to understand in ways the Gemini and Apple Intelligence controls currently are not. At launch, we found the settings to control Siri AI’s app access behavior pretty confusing . You had to toggle several options to block Siri AI off from accessing an app, or disable Siri AI entirely. Turning off Siri AI and reverting to Siri Classic is, for now, still a good option if you’d prefer to use the older version. The most recent update is far more clear and does more to protect your data. And, just as expected, it comes at the cost of some features. That’s a good thing, actually. The features not working shows that the new setting is effective. Here’s how to add apps to the exclusion list, once you’ve updated to 27.2: Open Settings > Siri > Excluded Apps Tap “Add Apps” and select any apps you’d like to add to the exclusion list Now Siri AI cannot access the contents of the app. Excluding an app also means you may lose some features. For example, if you exclude the Apple Messages app, you will no longer be able to have Siri AI read or respond to messages for you. Even the “onscreen awareness” feature, where you invoke Siri and ask it for information about what you’re currently looking at, will not work anymore. For example, if you exclude Signal, you cannot invoke Siri and ask it to discern any information in the Signal app. You’ll just get these messages: What’s the State of This on Android? The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop. stories.title: Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?
stories.summary: AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here If your social media algorithms have clocked that you’re into video games, something strange will have happened in the past few weeks. Your feed, like mine, will have been full of clips of streamers playing bizarre mashups of popular video games . Skyrim in Minecraft. Halo, except the main character is Mario. Skate 2 in Call of Duty maps. A flood of professional-looking fan-coded game mods that are mildly interesting to look at for 30 seconds, but ultimately inconsequential. Would I download a mod that lets me play Wii Bowling inside a zombie shooter? No, but I am very interested in where they came from. Of course, the answer – or at least, most of the answer – is AI. After a week of researching this (thanks especially to Replay Mode on YouTube for this informative video , which set me down this track) I now understand that these mashup mods are not just AI-generated videos, but AI-assisted coding. Basically, as of a few weeks ago, Anthropic’s Claude has become extremely good at decompiling video game code. Games are written by humans in readable code and then compiled into binary 1s and 0s that the PC or console running it can read; decompiling is the reversal of that process, revealing a game’s source code, which humans can then edit and mess around with for fun. This used to be an extremely laborious process. But now it is not, because humans aren’t doing much of it any more. Continue reading...

stories.body:
Turkey’s central Anatolian plateau is one of the country’s most important agricultural regions, producing wheat, maize, sugar beet and other crops. Yet beneath its cultivated fields, the ground is becoming increasingly unstable.

Large sinkholes , some tens of metres wide and deep, have appeared across the Konya basin, swallowing farmland, and threatening nearby roads and settlements .

These collapses can occur suddenly, sometimes in fields that have been cultivated for generations. Around 20 are opening up every year, according to a recent study.

Known locally as obruks , sinkholes are not a new geological phenomenon. They have existed in the Konya basin for thousands of years, but they have become far more frequent over recent decades.

Konya’s sinkholes are consequently both a geological hazard and evidence of a wider water-management problem. The cavities beneath the fields are the product of geological processes extending over thousands of years. Their recent instability, however, is occurring within a groundwater system profoundly altered by human activity and increasingly exposed to drought .

As representatives of countries all over the world prepare to head to Turkey to discuss climate change at the UN’s Cop 31 conference, Ankara continues to grapple with this escalating environmental disaster at home.

The nation’s disaster and emergency management authority (AFAD) has recently documented 684 sinkholes across Konya, Karaman and Aksaray in Turkey’s agricultural heartlands.

Why are they there?

The growing number of sinkholes is often attributed to drought and climate change . But intensive groundwater extraction for agriculture can also increase the risk of collapse.

Decades of intensive agricultural irrigation have altered the conditions beneath the basin’s surface. Groundwater, which is the layer of water below the Earth’s surface, is also not being replenished during long, dry periods, which adds to the problem.

Konya is a closed drainage basin . This means water entering the basin does not flow towards the sea. It is stored underground, and accumulates in lakes and wetlands, or returns to the atmosphere through evaporation and plant transpiration.

Rainfall is relatively low here, and much of it falls outside the main growing season. Groundwater has, therefore, become indispensable to agriculture, particularly for irrigated maize, sugar beet and fodder crops.

Read more: Subsidence claims: after drought, ground can shrink, swell or even collapse when it rains – causing damage to homes

The difficulty is that demand for water has grown beyond the rate at which the aquifers, a body of porous rock or sediment saturated with groundwater, can recover. A recent regional study estimated an average annual loss of groundwater storage, equivalent to 3.4 centimetres of water. This figure clearly points to a system under sustained pressure.

Part of the problem is that Turkey experienced its most severe drought for decades in 2025, putting more pressure on farmers.

Farmers often respond by extracting more groundwater, causing underground water levels to fall. This reduces the pressure exerted by water within the pores and fractures of rocks and sediments, potentially destabilising existing underground cavities and increasing the risk of collapse .

The consequences extend beyond water scarcity, because groundwater also puts stress on underground geological formations. The Konya basin contains extensive carbonate rocks, including limestone. Over long periods, groundwater circulating through fractures dissolves minerals and enlarges openings. This process, known as karstification , can produce underground channels, caves and cavities. Sinkholes form when the material above such voids becomes unstable.

Lower groundwater levels can also change the movement of water and sediment through existing underground cavities, allowing loose material to shift downwards. Where the roof of a cavity is already weak, these changes may eventually lead to collapse.

But the response is highly dependent on local conditions. The depth and shape of underground cavities, the thickness and strength of the layers of rock and sediment above them, the distribution of fractures and the history of groundwater fluctuations all matter.

This helps explain an important finding from a study on sinkhole formation in the Konya basin between 2000 and 2024. The researchers identified a sharp increase in the annual formation rate, from approximately three sinkholes a year during 2000-10 to 32 during 2016-19. Yet the rate subsequently declined to around 22 a year after 2020, despite continuing groundwater depletion.

If falling groundwater is responsible, why would fewer sinkholes form while water levels continue to decline? One possible explanation is that the most vulnerable cavities in some areas have already collapsed. Sinkhole formation depends on the number of unstable underground structures, not simply on the volume of water extracted.

Land is breaking down

The basin is also experiencing another type of ground deformation, known as land subsidence, in which the surface gradually sinks as underground sediments compact. This can cause cracks in the ground and damage to roads and buildings, although the sinking is often too gradual to notice without satellite measurements.

Satellite radar measurements revealed widespread land subsidence in the area, of up to 90 millimetres per year. Unlike sudden sinkhole collapse, this can develop as groundwater withdrawal increases stress on the land and compresses sediments in the ground.

The problem is not unique to Turkey. A global analysis estimated that over 6.3 million square kilometres of land are subsiding by more than five millimetres annually. The researchers identified groundwater extraction as the most influential factor worldwide.

In Konya, the pressure on groundwater is closely connected to agricultural production . Farmers cultivate crops for established markets and processing industries, often under policies that have favoured high levels of production, rather than water conservation.

Irrigation provides a way for farmers to maintain yields of crops during dry years, but it also allows production to continue at levels that the basin’s renewable water supply may not sustain.

However, restricting how much groundwater is extracted without providing support for farmers could impose substantial economic pressure on them, as well as on the nation’s food supply. But continued groundwater depletion could progressively undermine the agricultural production that made the region economically important in the first place.

More efficient irrigation could help, but is not enough. If water saved through improved technology is used to expand the area being irrigated, total groundwater consumption may remain unchanged or even increase.

A long-term response would require reliable monitoring of groundwater levels and withdrawals, enforceable extraction limits, agricultural incentives aligned with local water availability and detailed mapping of geological hazards. Satellite measurements can help identify areas under pressure.

The most immediate danger is that another field, road or building may collapse, putting lives at risk.

Preventing the next sinkhole is difficult. The government could address the problem. But it needs to introduce agricultural policies that treat groundwater as a finite resource, rather than a permanent substitute for rainfall.

Reporting Highlights

Scientists’ Secret Vote: A U.N. climate report legitimized carbon capture and storage, suggesting at least 99% of the CO2 would likely remain underground, despite scant empirical evidence.

Oil Industry Favorite: Fossil fuel companies have identified carbon capture as a climate solution that will allow their industry to survive, and have pushed the U.N. and scientists to study it.

Pattern of Underperformance: Decades later, major CO2 storage projects have suffered breakdowns, setbacks and cost overruns, while CCS remains central to climate models and policy.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

In the spring of 2005, the United Nations convened more than 100 of the world’s top scientists in the medieval town of Oviedo, Spain. They were there to finish writing a paradigm-shifting report about a technology that they hoped could help stop climate change.

To celebrate the report’s impending completion, the meeting’s hosts handed out bottles of cava, Spanish sparkling wine, with tongue-in-cheek labels stating that they were to be opened only by those who truly believed it could work.

Belief was necessary because the technology — carbon capture and storage, or CCS — had barely been tested. The idea was simple: strip carbon dioxide from smokestacks before it could flow into the air and warm the planet. Then pump it into a porous part of the Earth’s crust and leave it there. Forever.

The experts in Oviedo had stacks of papers proving that parts of the process worked. But major questions remained about how much space exists inside the Earth to store the CO2, how effectively it could be monitored and whether the poisonous, concentrated gas would reliably stay underground.

Tasked with wrangling roughly three dozen of those scientists toward consensus was Sally Benson, a geoscientist from Lawrence Berkeley National Lab who was co-leading the report’s chapter on underground storage of carbon. After a quarter-century of studying how fluids and gases move beneath Earth’s surface, she was an unimpeachable authority on the subject. She was also a savvy and diplomatic leader, skilled at managing rooms full of big egos and big tempers. It was proving handy in a process that had at times devolved into unruly debate.

The scientists had clashed for years over what the report should say, first at a meeting in Canada, then in Norway, Australia and Brazil. The evidence was scant. Three large-scale experiments were underway, but only one — a Norwegian operation that captured carbon from a natural gas field and pumped it under the bed of the North Sea — had rigorously tested permanent storage. There, the injected CO2 astonished engineers when it floated 700 feet upward through a series of geologic formations. To their relief, it hit a ceiling of shale that kept it underground, and the project was deemed a success. But with so little to go on, the scientists warned in their first draft that any broad statement about leakage risk would be “almost meaningless.”

The researchers were in Oviedo only because Saudi Arabia and other oil-exporting countries had pressured the U.N. to write the report despite the paucity of evidence, according to U.N. officials and records. The oil, gas and coal industries had spent years casting doubt on climate change while quietly fretting that policies to address it would one day put them out of business. The industry, documents show, saw CCS as a way to forestall that outcome, allowing the world to keep burning fossil fuels while simply burying the pollution underground. A U.N. report would bring the technology into the mainstream.

In turn, the U.N. hoped such a report would draw the oil-producing nations into its search for climate solutions. So despite objections from some nations and environmental organizations, which warned that the report would distract from the imperative to phase out fossil fuels, the U.N.’s preeminent climate science authority, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, went ahead. And for the first time, it invited a large contingent of industry researchers to join the scientists in writing the report, as well as several representatives from environmental groups. Benson’s chapter included authors and editors from Shell, Chevron and Saudi Aramco.

The process that followed would make some of the chapter’s scientists uneasy. The IPCC’s procedures stated that reports should assess the existing research on a topic based on peer-reviewed literature and that exceptions must be reviewed and clearly cited.

Bert Metz, one of the highest-ranking U.N. officials at the meeting, was pressing the group to come up with more definitive language about CCS’ potential. The report would be better if it could offer hard numbers, even where none existed in the literature: Precisely how many gigatons of storage capacity did the planet likely have? How long would a well-designed reservoir hold the CO2 injected into it? More than a year? A thousand years?

With so little evidence to work with, David Keith, a Canadian physicist, proposed a workaround: The authors could conduct an “expert elicitation,” taking an anonymous survey about what they expected the evidence to eventually show.

At first, not everyone was willing to go along. Some scientists worried that making what amounted to educated guesses would mislead the public, they told Drilled and ProPublica. Benson and Metz, though, both argued that on such an important matter informed advice was better than nothing.

In the end, the group agreed to take the survey and to keep it off the record — they would “burn it afterward,” Keith recounted, making no mention of it in the official report. When the meeting concluded, some of the scientists popped their bottles of cava in celebration.

“It’s not the hard science that you would prefer, obviously,” Metz would later tell Drilled and ProPublica.

Five months later, the IPCC published its special report, which would help legitimize CCS for a generation.

The 431-page document portrayed CCS as a potential savior for the climate that could enable countries “to continue to include fossil fuels in their energy mix.” It stated that using CCS could lower the cost of stabilizing global CO2 concentrations by at least 30% and that if fully supported by policy, it could account for as much as 55% of the world’s efforts to limit climate change through this century.

It acknowledged that there were still gaps in research and experience with the technology — offering extensive detail deep within its pages about the challenges and uncertainties of piecing together separate but proven steps in the CCS process. But its summary stated that “there are no major technical or knowledge barriers” to storing captured CO2 underground.

All of those assertions, however, rested on the critical determinations made by the scientists handling the storage chapter.

Benson’s group wrote that the planet offered vast CO2 storage capacity. Storage sites that were well selected and well managed, they said, were likely to retain 99% of the carbon pumped into them for at least 1,000 years.

A Consequential Decision

The scientists’ conclusions that day in Spain have had profound, compounding consequences.

The special report has been cited in thousands of academic papers, in legislative testimony and in media coverage validating carbon capture and storage as a realistic solution to global warming.

When climate forecasters built models, their calculations assumed CCS would work. When governments and corporations began making so-called “net zero” pledges, promising to subtract as much CO2 from the atmosphere as they add, they assumed CCS would work. When policymakers gave energy companies billions of dollars in public funds to develop “clean coal,” they assumed CCS would work.

These presumptions shifted the world’s discourse from how to limit carbon pollution to how to remove it from the atmosphere after the fact.

Enthusiasm for the technology has only grown. This spring, California embarked on one of the world’s largest carbon burial endeavors yet. While President Donald Trump eviscerated most programs addressing the climate, he has expanded subsidies for CCS. There are more than 100 applications for storage sites pending in the U.S. alone. U.N. analyses suggest that to achieve environmental goals, a CCS industry the size of the entire global oil production industry would have to be built by 2050.

But 21 years after Oviedo, a staggering gap lies between expectations for the technology and its operational reality. Since 1996, just 12 large-scale geological storage projects have been constructed. Collectively, they bury less CO2 than a single power plant can emit in a year, according to our analysis of sites listed in an International Energy Agency database . Seven of them have faced technical, financial or performance issues. An investigation by Drilled and ProPublica found there’s reason to doubt carbon capture and storage will ever succeed at the scale needed to offer a significant climate solution.
