Why Carbon Capture Can’t Conceivably Solve Climate Change

History is full of audacious technological leaps — moments when visionary engineering solved seemingly intractable problems. Scientists told Drilled and ProPublica that they have devoted themselves to studying CCS in that spirit, hoping a grand techno-fix could help the world solve the climate crisis without a painful overhaul of the global energy system.

But that ambition did not exist in isolation. It was bankrolled in large part by companies that stood to profit from its success.

Industry documents show that oil company executives have long seen CCS as a way to hedge against climate regulation, greenwash their brands and preserve their core business. Internal Exxon documents obtained by Drilled and ProPublica show that in 1988, the company determined that any climate research Exxon supported should serve the dual purposes of protecting the value of its oil, gas and coal while preserving the company’s business options; the company would eventually become one of the world’s major funders of CCS research.

Later, the American Petroleum Institute would write in internal communications that the industry’s “license to operate” depended on companies lowering climate pollution, and CCS, it wrote, “enables the use of petroleum and natural gas by providing an opportunity to capture and/or offset emissions.” And at a 2023 prominent oil industry conference in Houston, the CEO of Occidental Petroleum, Vicki Hollub, would explain that a novel form of CCS that sucks carbon directly from the air “is going to be the technology that helps to preserve our industry over time.”

For many university faculty, the rewards for studying the industry’s favored climate solution have been numerous, opening opportunities, funding papers and raising their profiles. Benson is a clear example. When the IPCC was awarded in 2007 with the Nobel Peace Prize for its climate work, she and her co-authors were recognized among the scientists who contributed. When Stanford University sought a new director for its ExxonMobil-funded climate research center, it tapped her. When President Joe Biden prioritized climate policy, he brought Benson into the White House.

Keith, the Canadian physicist, benefited from oil industry interest in a different way: He developed technology to capture CO2. Occidental Petroleum paid more than $1 billion to buy the company he founded.

There is no evidence that Benson, widely described by colleagues as scrupulous, skewed her scientific findings to suit the interests of her industry patrons, and Benson has described CCS’ flaws in her publications.

However, in speeches, presentations and even congressional testimony, she has been a dogged champion of CCS technology, time and again describing it as safe and ready for large-scale deployment, despite having a ringside view to its many setbacks.

She has frequently referenced the most affirmative statements from her group’s work in Oviedo as evidence. But the methodology Benson and her co-authors used to reach those conclusions 21 years ago has not been generally understood. When Drilled and ProPublica told prominent climate researchers about the expert elicitation process, several were disconcerted to learn that there was so little scientific basis for the report’s conclusion that 99% of CO2 was likely to remain underground.

A survey, said Oliver Geden, a vice chair of the IPCC’s forthcoming climate assessment, was “an inappropriate way of assessing the literature.”

Authors “are not supposed to do original research. They’re supposed to just collect what’s out there,” said Roger Cooke, who was a lead author on a subsequent IPCC report. Cooke said expert elicitation, done rigorously, can be valuable, but “just asking a bunch of experts to give their best guess is one of the worst things you can do.”

In a detailed written response, Benson said she did not believe that the survey undertaken in 2005 violated IPCC norms and said the group’s leadership was aware of the process. She disputed that the approach amounted to an informed guess and said that “there was an enormous amount of data” to draw on. The group was trying to agree on the best language to synthesize evidence detailed deeper in the report. She rejected the notion that her research or career were influenced by industry funding, writing that she has worked “tirelessly for 30 years on CCS and other climate solutions” in a sincere effort to combat an escalating planetary crisis. And, she offered, she views CCS as one valuable tool among many needed to address climate change.

Keith said the goal of the expert elicitation was not to seek precision, but to provide a sense of the orders of magnitude of the capacity and risks, “because that’s what’s relevant to public policy.” He said even sites with problems haven’t leaked large amounts of CO2 and that the report’s broad statements “have stood the test of time.” The chapter authors’ confidence in CCS doesn’t suggest “that a bunch of us are tools of the fossil fuel industry.”

The IPCC declined to comment on specific questions about how the report came about. “We are not in a position to comment on individual recollections,” a spokesperson wrote about the expert elicitation. However, they said that the group’s process was in keeping with the organization’s procedures at the time and that it reflected contemporaneous understanding of the technology. The IPCC did not directly respond to the assertion that the authors conducted what amounts to new research during the writing process, and it did not provide requested records that would detail the scientists’ vote. “The IPCC’s role is to assess the full range of available scientific knowledge,” the statement said. Metz referred to the IPCC’s response.

Chevron, Shell and Saudi Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

Drilled and ProPublica spoke with more than 100 experts on carbon capture, climate modeling and influence in academia, including a dozen people who attended the Oviedo meeting. We compiled records of geologic storage tests and surveyed an extensive body of peer-reviewed literature. This investigation is part of a broader examination into how fossil fuel industry funding of climate research has shaped climate policy, solutions and public understanding. It follows our report in June about a BP-funded program at Princeton University and the oil company’s role in crafting one of the program’s most influential climate papers.

Since Benson and her co-authors met in Oviedo, weather catastrophes have multiplied, oceans have acidified and the amount of carbon in the atmosphere has soared. In September, the U.N. released an urgent new report declaring that the race to avert disruptive warming has been all but lost. It concluded that “overshoot” — the notion that temperatures will rise above the world’s adopted goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming — is now a certainty.

Carbon capture and storage, it said, is one of the only ways to bring those temperatures back down.

Looking at a Failure and Calling It Triumph

Just a few days before the meeting in Oviedo, BP put Benson and a handful of other scientists on a chartered flight from London to Algeria. Their destination: the world’s second major geologic carbon storage experiment, in the Sahara.

The British oil giant, along with the state-owned oil companies of Algeria and Norway, had begun to drill for gas at a new field named for a nearby oasis called In Salah. Most natural gas comes out of the ground as a cocktail of methane and CO2. The CO2 must be stripped out and is usually vented into the sky. But at In Salah, the companies saw an opportunity to try out a greener process — one that could become big business.

Earth’s crust is a layer cake of rock. Some layers, like sandstone, contain honeycombed pores capable of holding CO2, while others, like mudstone, can act as impermeable seals, trapping the buoyant gas underground.

That layer cake is impossible to precisely chart from the surface, but engineers sent sound waves into the ground and interpreted what echoed up into rough maps. They learned their target sandstone reservoir sat below a 3,000-foot-thick brick of mudstone they believed would be impermeable. They also learned the sandstone was “tight” — less honeycombed than they had hoped — but still capable of holding gas. So they had begun to inject the CO2.

The plane landed on a sand-strewn strip circled by jeep tracks and rocky plateaus. A photograph shows Benson, medium height, her blond bob tucked beneath a hard hat, standing in the desert alongside a BP-funded physicist from Princeton named Robert Socolow and seven other men in front of a well that was pushing CO2 under the desert. In Salah had been operating for less than a year but seemed to be going smoothly.

Afterward, Benson traveled to Oviedo to finish drafting the special report, which listed In Salah among key sites that “indicate that it is feasible to store CO2” underground at significant scale.

That assessment has not held up.

Energy companies had first begun pumping CO2 into the ground commercially in the 1970s, when they realized it would loosen up stubborn crude oil, sometimes doubling an oil field’s output. They called it “enhanced oil recovery,” and though they didn’t try to lock the CO2 in place, much of it seemed to stay underground.

The idea to use carbon injection as a climate fix came a few years later from an Italian physicist named Cesare Marchetti, who suggested disposing of carbon deep in the ocean or underground. In the 1980s Exxon tried, and gave up on, efforts to develop the idea. And it wasn’t until 1996 when the first large-scale CCS project — the operation in the North Sea — began.

In a recent interview inside her narrow, fluorescent-lit office at Stanford University’s earth sciences building, Benson said it was shortly after that that she first heard of CCS. A colleague at the Department of Energy had sent her a slide deck by Princeton’s Socolow about the technology. “I was like, ‘I think this is nuts,’” she told Drilled and ProPublica.

“I just couldn’t really picture it working at scale.”

But, as both an idealist and a pragmatist, she was drawn to the potential for science to solve difficult environmental problems. She made a crude calculation of how much CO2 might fit beneath California and was surprised by the answer: a lot. At least in theory. And it changed her mind.

As Benson became one of CCS’ leading experts and champions, she increasingly found herself in rooms full of oil industry veterans. In 2000, she helped establish a partnership between the Department of Energy and companies including Chevron, Texaco and BP. That program had a focused mission: make large-scale geological storage an operational reality by 2015.

In 2002, Benson was asked to sit on the advisory council of a new BP and Ford Motor Co.-funded climate research center at Princeton University. At a summit there the following year, Benson expressed concern that focusing on leaks could undermine public support for CCS, according to meeting records and the account of another person in attendance.

“Need to present optimistic estimates,” the minutes recapping her presentation say.

By 2007, Benson was helping to run her own industry-funded research center. A few years earlier, ExxonMobil CEO Lee Raymond, a thunderous voice of climate denial, had put up $100 million of the company’s money to fund climate and energy work at Stanford University. With another $125 million from three other companies, Stanford’s Global Climate and Energy Project became one of the best-funded climate research centers in America.

The donation came with strings: ExxonMobil and the other sponsors had veto power over which research projects received funding.

Students and activists protested the funding structure, accusing ExxonMobil of retracing the path of tobacco companies, which paid for scientific work on obscure causes of cancer as a distraction from their culpability.

Benson defended the arrangement ardently and often. ExxonMobil and the other sponsors approved every grant that Stanford recommended, never exercising their veto power, she said. Reporting by Drilled and ProPublica did not contradict that assertion. Benson also pointed to the fact that the program funded an array of research, including on renewable energy.

In an interview and written response, Benson said researchers who take funding from oil companies are motivated not by corporate agendas, but by genuine interest in the work. The funding underwrites the inquiry, she said, not its conclusions. Where there’s “alignment,” she added, the industry support can be “amazingly catalytic and helpful.”

In response to a request for comment, Stanford University directed Drilled and ProPublica to former law school dean Paul Brest, who led a committee that reviewed energy research funding at the school. Brest said that faculty have a right to seek any funding they choose, so long as sponsors cannot direct the work.

Most important to Benson was that scientists and their students have the opportunity to research matters of great consequence. She has published more than 50 papers on geologic carbon storage since joining Stanford, most of them highly technical evaluations of CCS that reiterated its importance to reducing emissions, and many underwritten by ExxonMobil and other industry sources. “I don’t know anybody else,” she told Drilled and ProPublica, “who would eventually provide, you know, $225 million of funding” to study climate solutions.

But whether researchers intended to serve their funders’ agenda on CCS or not, some say the effect has been undeniable. “It seems like a credible solution because you have credible people at credible institutions working on it,” said Naomi Oreskes, a Harvard historian of science and an expert in corporate influence.

Benson was still getting settled into her new job at Stanford when the project in Algeria ran into major problems.

On a 118-degree day in 2007, In Salah’s inspectors heard CO2 whistling through the top of an abandoned oil well nearly a mile from the nearest injection site. Engineers had believed it would take years before the CO2 plume could spread so far underground, but the gas had cracked through the sandstone and found a new path.

To stop the leak, workers poured cement into the well, plugging it permanently. But soon a second problem arose: Satellite data revealed the desert floor above the injection sites had bulged. When project engineers again used sound waves and other tools to map the layers underground, they arrived at an alarming discovery: Pressurized CO2 had sent cracks a quarter of the way up through the 3000-foot-thick layer of mudstone. If it breached the rest, it could leach into the pan-Saharan aquifer, acidifying a source of drinking water millions of people depend on.

BP and its partners eventually summoned Benson and the other science advisers to London. The dangerous gas, they could now see, was moving in ways they had predicted it could not. Nonetheless, the advisers suggested that injection proceed temporarily to see whether it could safely be done under lower pressure and with careful monitoring.

But the Algerians had had enough. In 2011 BP and its partners stopped injection, and in 2012 they quietly scrapped the project.

Benson would later describe In Salah as a technical failure but a triumph of detection. “It was monitored and people found a problem,” she told Drilled and ProPublica.

“Then,” she added, they “learned from it.”

More Problems, More Dependence

As she did in Oviedo, Benson still maintains that the fundamental mechanics of CCS are well enough understood to know that it can work.

As proof that geologic formations can handle high-pressure gas, she points to the natural gas industry, which injects large amounts of its product back underground for temporary storage.

She also points to enhanced oil recovery. Over the last 40 years, American companies have injected 100 times more CO2 into drilling fields as a way to extract more oil than they have into what CCS industry insiders call “dedicated” CO2 storage reservoirs. There are few reports of accidents or leaks at these sites.

Unlike dedicated CO2 storage, though, enhanced oil recovery is less likely to cause pressure to build up underground, because the CO2 pumped in fills space left by the oil that’s forced out. (These sites also can result in a net addition of CO2 in the atmosphere, since they wind up producing still more oil.)

The record of the industry’s largest CCS sites — ones designed solely to help the climate — has been far more troubled.

Around the time In Salah shut down, the world’s third large project — a Norwegian site named Snøhvit several hundred miles north of the Arctic Circle — also met critical obstacles. When injection began in 2008, engineers had calculated the site would have an 18-year capacity. But they had radically overestimated how much CO2 it could absorb and had to relocate the project after just three years.

In the U.S., a decadelong effort to build a “clean coal” power plant outfitted with CCS proved impossible within a reasonable budget and was abandoned in 2015 — but not before the government had spent $378 million in taxpayer money. Benson was on the project’s advisory board for part of that time.

That year in Canada, Shell opened a $1 billion carbon capture and storage facility — also largely paid for by the country’s taxpayers — connected to open-pit oil sands mines. The industry routinely promises that plants like this one, called Quest, capture at least 90% of emissions. But at Quest, once the energy required for the capture process itself is accounted for, the capture rate instead has hovered around 68%, according to a report by the research group Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. It has also caused hundreds of microearthquakes.

Shell did not respond to a request for comment.

As one carbon storage project struggled after another, Benson and other academic researchers continued to insist they could flourish.

In a keynote speech at a 2018 conference in Sweden, Benson showed a slide with a map of CCS facilities across the world, most of which were enhanced oil recovery sites. Her map included In Salah, which had shuttered. And it included another project, in Australia, which had yet to open. “The operations have been very good at all of these projects. And they’ve gone well in terms of safety,” she said.

She also showed a slide pointing to the 2005 U.N. special report’s statement that an “appropriately selected,” well-managed reservoir would likely retain 99% of its carbon for more than 1,000 years. “This was an expression that if you find the right site, the CO2 should be permanently stored,” she said.

In a written response, she said she continues to cite the 21-year-old special report’s conclusions on leakage because “the methodology was sound then and remains so.” Benson said that she is careful to qualify her characterizations and show evidence in her presentations, and that during her presentation in Sweden she did so. She did not directly address the status of projects portrayed in her map.

When the Australian project, called Gorgon, did open the following year, it turned out to be the biggest CCS fiasco yet. Australia had allowed Chevron, ExxonMobil and Shell to drill a major new natural gas field there with the requirement that the companies buried at least 80% of the CO2 that came out of the ground with it. It was billed as the world’s largest CCS operation.

Instead, it has been plagued by clogged injection wells and underground pressure spikes. In their operating year ending in 2025, the companies were able to inject just a quarter of the CO2 collected there. Since they vent the remainder, Gorgon, once billed as a model for climate solutions, became the largest single source of industrial carbon pollution on the continent.

“Like any pioneering endeavour, it takes time to optimise a new system to ensure it performs reliably over 40-plus years of operation,” a Chevron spokesperson wrote in an emailed response. “We realise that people refer to the challenges at Gorgon in an attempt to discredit CCS, however, as we have shown, we can capture and store greenhouse gas at scale.” Shell and ExxonMobil did not respond to requests for comment.

An Idea Takes Root

While operators struggled to prove CCS could be viable, the world became dependent on it working.

As soon as the IPCC published the 2005 report, climate modelers that help assess the most economic ways to limit global warming began folding CCS into their calculations.

They projected not only that CCS could stop billions of tons of emissions from reaching the sky, but that it could suck old carbon pollution out of the atmosphere. They adopted a theory that supposed vast fields of switchgrass or fast-growing willow could absorb carbon into their stalks and leaves, and when those plants were harvested and burned for electricity, their emissions, too, would be captured and buried.

The modelers incorporated this subtractive approach so prodigiously that, on paper, they could reverse climate change. Global temperatures could overshoot targets in the short term, so long as enough carbon was eventually sucked back out of the air to bring those temperatures back down.

World leaders embraced the wiggle room this theory provided them. When they signed the U.N. Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, pledging to keep warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, they counted on these so-called negative emissions among the key tools that could make it possible. In 2018, when the IPCC published a special report on how to reach that goal, 89 out of its 90 scenarios included using large-scale CCS.

Now, in its latest report , the U.N. says that it is virtually impossible to still get to a 1.5 C future — or anything close — without removing carbon from the atmosphere. There are several ways to do that — reforestation and the use of minerals spread on fields to absorb carbon, for instance. But these methods are either small scale or even less proven than CCS.

By 2015, the tantalizing idea of “negative emissions” was showing up in new, mainstream ways. “Net zero” pledges to one day offset carbon emissions began rolling in from most of the world’s nations, as well as cities like Omaha, Nebraska; the band Coldplay; ice cream chains; funeral homes; and even ExxonMobil.

But real-world CCS projects have not met the moment.

To scale the technology as much as U.N. analyses suggest is needed to limit warming to 2 C would require not only a technological feat but almost unimaginable resources, Drilled and ProPublica found . Carbon dioxide injection would have to almost immediately increase by more than 400 times. That would require more than 2,000 new geological waste sites to be established — a new large-scale CCS project put into operation every four days, on average, for the next 25 years.

To move the CO2 to those sites would require 68,000 miles of specialized pipeline in the U.S. alone. Globally, at least 85 custom-built tankers would be needed to carry the high-pressure gas safely across oceans. Just four exist.

And if all of that were accomplished, the effort would come at an almost inconceivable cost: tens of trillions of dollars.

“Fuck, OK, It’s Harder Than We Thought”

At Benson’s office at Stanford, in a building where rocks painstakingly collected from field sites fill cabinets in the halls, the Society of Petroleum Engineers hosts Friday socials — beer and snacks provided — and the adjacent courtyard is named after the oil company Arco.

Inside, propped on a stack of boxes, is a framed copy of Biden’s keystone climate legislation, the Inflation Reduction Act. On it, national climate adviser Ali Zaidi scrawled in blue sharpie, “Thank you, Sally, for helping truly transform our energy & climate future!”

Benson returned to Stanford after a nearly two-year stint in Biden’s White House as the head of the energy division of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, where she says she provided periodic scientific advice as the act was being pushed through Congress. One of the most ambitious climate policy efforts in history, it offered a large set of incentives for CCS, which the fossil fuel industry had lobbied for intensely.

But even while oil industry leaders have pushed the world to embrace CCS, behind closed doors, they have remained skeptical of its potential as a climate solution.

In 2007, as ExxonMobil funded Benson’s center at Stanford, its former CEO Raymond told a room full of industry leaders that carbon storage might be considered “kind of the Holy Grail.” Executing it, though, would be “a whole different animal” than injecting carbon underground for enhanced oil recovery. “You can’t assume that’s going to happen. And the cost is going to be very, very significant.”

A 2011 internal slide deck from BP stated that while carbon storage would allow fossil fuels to remain the world’s dominant source of energy, “the pace of CCS development has been slow and the future pace remains uncertain.” And in a 2018 internal presentation , ExxonMobil predicted hardly any CCS would be deployed by 2050, even as it modeled that global CO2 emissions from energy production would continue to skyrocket.

Yet the industry saw brand value in encouraging CCS anyway. An ExxonMobil document from 2021 describes a public relations campaign to persuade the political and financial “elites” to “believe ExxonMobil is committed to helping solve climate change,” in part by proving its efforts on CCS will “play an indispensable role” in a greener economy.

For her part, Benson still has faith in the technology’s viability, despite the failures. “These are big projects, right? The idea that everything goes exactly according to plan, especially for these first-of-a-kind projects — it’s unrealistic.”

As proof that CCS is on the rise, she pointed to 77 operating CCS projects identified in a report by the industry group the Global CCS Institute and said that another report demonstrated a tenfold growth in CO2 injected underground since 2005.

When ProPublica and Drilled reviewed that same data, however, and excluded the enhanced oil recovery projects, we found just eight operating large-scale carbon burial projects on that list (10 using the group’s more recent data), and half the increase in annual injections that Benson stated.

Experts interviewed for this story insisted — often in an anguished timbre — that CCS simply must work because decades of delay have foreclosed other paths to a stable climatic future.

But just because the world now needs CCS to work doesn’t mean it can.

“It’s always some issue,” said Glen Peters, a senior researcher at the Cicero Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “I think there’s been a lack of willingness for the community to say, ‘Fuck, OK, it’s harder than we thought.’”

The latest CCS effort got underway this spring, in California, when the oil company California Resources Corp. began injecting CO2 beneath the state’s Central Valley.

California — long a vanguard of environmental policy — has embraced the technology. In 2021, as it was formulating a plan for how the state should reach its climate targets, the California Air Resources Board invited Benson to give a presentation on the role CCS could play .

“The fraction of CO2 retained underground is likely to be very high,” she told the board, again pointing to the 2005 special report: “This study said 99% over 1,000 years.”

The board set the ambitious goal of burying more than 100 million tons of CO2 a year by 2045, more than all the carbon that has ever been geologically stored around the world combined. Since it opened in May, the new project has injected just 7% of its advertised capacity, but California Resources Corp. is now seeking permits for eight more CCS projects across California, and other oil and gas companies have proposed four more, including two that Stanford is directly involved with.

California Resources Corp., in a written response, said the company is injecting the amount it had planned for early operations and will increase to capacity as the project develops.

Could California truly be burying 100 million tons of CO2 a year by 2045? For the first time, in an interview, Benson was hesitant to commit. “I think it’s very challenging,” she said. “That’s a lot of infrastructure, a lot of money, a lot of projects.”

Asked a second time, she once again demurred. “Oh gosh. If we really set our mind to it. If we could wave a wand.”

stories.title: Federal and State Officials Ramp Up Scrutiny of DraftKings, Other Sports Betting Apps
stories.summary: The post Federal and State Officials Ramp Up Scrutiny of DraftKings, Other Sports Betting Apps appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Amid investigations by ProPublica and others, officials across the country are demanding information about how online sportsbooks entice customers to keep betting — and proposing new rules to help protect consumers.

State and federal officials have ramped up scrutiny of online sports betting companies in recent weeks, launching inquiries, demanding information and, in one case, proposing a new rule that would limit when companies like DraftKings can pitch their users to bet more.

The moves — by gaming regulators, government lawyers and federal lawmakers — follow an investigation last month by ProPublica that tested the guardrails DraftKings and other sports betting companies have in place to protect users from spiraling out of control. That system is called responsible gaming, and executives say it’s integral to their companies’ long-term success.

The ProPublica article showed how DraftKings bestowed VIP status on a reporter who deliberately bet like a problem gambler . The report detailed the ways in which the app’s user design and promotions encouraged more betting — even after the reporter opted into responsible gaming tools designed to slow users down. A week earlier, The New York Times reported that DraftKings had used machine learning and artificial intelligence to target promotions to losing bettors .

Those articles were the focus of an Oct. 15 meeting of the Louisiana Gaming Control Board , which, partly in response to the stories, tabled the renewal of DraftKings’ five-year license. Instead, the board granted the company a temporary four-month permit while investigators look into the issues raised in the reports as well as other paperwork concerns.

The board’s chair, Christopher Hebert, said the Times had raised some “very serious questions” and called ProPublica’s reporting “very troubling.”

While news stories “are not findings of regulatory violations,” Hebert said, “as regulators we have a responsibility to examine these matters that could affect the integrity of gaming operations and the protections of our citizens here in Louisiana.”

State health officials say the number of Louisianans believed to have a gambling disorder has risen in recent years amid the surge in popularity of online gambling and prediction market sites. One top official reported this summer that gambling addiction was among the health department’s “top three priorities.”

What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out.

If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files.

Paul Liberman, who co-founded DraftKings and serves as its president of operations, told the regulators: “We do not use artificial intelligence to target losing gamblers by any means.”

DraftKings previously told ProPublica that it proactively closes the accounts of suspected problem gamblers “all the time” but declined to provide specific figures. Yet when asked by a Louisiana board member for those same specifics, Lori Kalani, DraftKings’ chief responsible gaming officer, said 175 accounts in the state had been shut down this year. She told the board she didn’t know how many total users DraftKings had in the Pelican State.

“We’re not physicians, we’re not clinicians and that’s not our role, but we certainly want to help people enjoy the service, the platform that we’re offering them,” Kalani told the board. “I know that we’re doing our job and that when we see something, we say something and we engage. I just can’t tell you if 175 is the right number. I wish it was zero.”

In a statement, a DraftKings spokesperson said: “As a legal, regulated operator, DraftKings values an open and ongoing dialogue with regulators and regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business.”

In response to ProPublica’s original investigation, Kalani said DraftKings’ responsible gaming system — which consists largely of in-app messages about the company’s tools — “worked the way it was supposed to.” She cautioned against “drawing broad conclusions” from one user’s experience.

The day after the Louisiana meeting, regulators in Ohio proposed an amendment to the state’s sports gaming rule that would bar companies like DraftKings from sending direct ads or marketing to bettors for 48 hours after they’d opted into responsible gaming tools or updated their current settings.

The proposed amendment speaks directly to a finding in ProPublica’s reporting: After blowing nearly $4,500 betting on tennis in 24 hours, the reporter used such tools to limit the amount of time and money he could spend on the app. Just 30 minutes later, though, he received the first of four push notifications promoting new betting opportunities. It wasn’t until he opted into a far more restrictive tool, called a “cool-off,” that the notifications temporarily stopped.

Andromeda Morrison, the interim executive director of the Ohio Casino Control Commission, said that though her office had been working on its proposal for some time, ProPublica’s story illuminated the issue. “Hopefully this is something that is fairly easy for the industry to see as a common sense restriction to make sure those consumers are making good choices without those push notifications,” she said.

But Keith Whyte, a former director of the National Council on Problem Gambling who now consults for industry and nonprofit groups, said the proposed amendment could unintentionally disincentivize users from using tools like deposit limits. “I think the implication is that using a responsible gaming tool is a sign of a gambling problem,” he said. The measure faces a long rulemaking process, including more rounds of public hearings and comments.

Sports betting operators are also feeling the heat at the federal level.

Citing ProPublica’s reporting, three Democrats who have long called for industry reforms are now demanding more information from major sports betting and prediction market companies about how the businesses entice their customers.

The letters are signed by Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, New York Rep. Paul Tonko and North Carolina Rep. Valerie Foushee. They asked the companies to answer a series of questions, including how many customers are enrolled in their VIP programs and how much revenue is generated by them.

“As repeated stories from exploited gamblers and media reports have vividly documented, VIP programs are driving the gambling industry’s most susceptible customers into debt and addiction through rewards tied to waging ever increasing amounts of money,” the lawmakers wrote.

DraftKings conferred VIP status on a ProPublica reporter after he lost close to $6,000 in three weeks on the app by chasing losses with long-shot bets, playing late into the night and firing risky wagers on fast action, like whether a major league baseball player will take a strike, a ball or connect for a hit — betting behavior that experts say are clear red flags of problem gambling.

In a statement, DraftKings said it would “respond accordingly once we have had a chance to review” the letter. Its biggest competitor, FanDuel, which has been trading letters with the lawmakers for months, wrote on Oct. 20 that the company was committed to responsible gaming and said “the VIP program is intended to provide enhanced service and encourage customers who chose to wager to use FanDuel rather than another platform.”

The companies are likely to face further scrutiny.

Read More

In New York, investigators for the state’s attorney general have contacted former DraftKings employees about issues raised in the Times’ story, the newspaper reported, citing people familiar with the probe and messages it had reviewed. A spokesperson for the office declined to comment.

That inquiry follows proposals earlier this month by state gaming officials that they say will strengthen New York’s own standards governing the use of artificial intelligence and responsible gaming guidelines .

Regulators in Maine , Massachusetts and Michigan have also said that they’re reviewing some of those same issues.

DraftKings, the spokesperson said, “does not market to customers based on indicators of potential problem gaming.”

Still, there are signs that yet more states may be interested in vetting those claims.

Jennifer Davenport, New Jersey’s attorney general, recently told the RG Journal, a publication that focuses on responsible gaming and industry matters , that “we are monitoring recent press reports alleging certain sports books are ignoring our consumer safeguards and chasing customers who are clearly exhibiting signs of problem betting.”

“Let them be warned, our office stands ready to take action against anyone who violates our gaming regulations and tries taking advantage of New Jerseyans and those who gamble here,” she said.

A spokesperson for Davenport declined to comment.

stories.body:
De nombreux gouvernements africains ont restreint l’accès aux réseaux sociaux lors de récentes tensions politiques ou sociales. Présentées comme des mesures de sécurité, ces décisions soulèvent la question de l’apaisement face à une crise par la suspension des espaces numériques où elle s’exprime.

Le 24 octobre 2026, le Gabon annonçait le rétablissement de plusieurs réseaux sociaux après plus de huit mois de suspension. Décidée en février dernier par la Haute autorité de la communication au nom de la sécurité nationale et de la stabilité institutionnelle, cette mesure avait notamment affecté Facebook, TikTok et YouTube. Sa levée intervient alors que les autorités renforcent par ailleurs la réglementation des usages numériques.

L’épisode pose une question qui dépasse le Gabon. Les réseaux sociaux facilitent la circulation des revendications, amplifient parfois les tensions et peuvent servir à diffuser des appels à la violence. Mais ils permettent aussi de s’informer, de documenter des événements et de discuter de l’action publique.

Les interrompre revient-il à réduire la crise, ou seulement à en modifier la visibilité ?

Chercheur en sciences de l’information et de la communication, je suis spécialiste des dynamiques informationnelles en situation de crise. À travers cette analyse, j’interroge l’efficacité des restrictions numériques en tant qu’instruments de gestion des crises sociales et politiques.

Une réponse qui dépasse l’Afrique

Au Sénégal , en 2023, l’accès à plusieurs plateformes, puis à Internet mobile, a été restreint lors de manifestations.

Au Mozambique , des restrictions similaires ont accompagné les contestations postélectorales de 2024.

En Tanzanie , Internet a été interrompu pendant plusieurs jours lors des élections d’octobre 2025 et des manifestations qui ont suivi.

Read more: Cameroun : une étude montre ce que les réseaux sociaux font à la politique – et vice-versa

Au-delà du continent africain, la France a également envisagé ce type de réponse. Le 4 juillet 2023, lors des émeutes consécutives à la mort de Nahel , Emmanuel Macron évoquait la possibilité de « réguler ou couper » les réseaux sociaux lorsque les violences s'intensifiaient.

Cette hypothèse n’a pas abouti à une coupure nationale. En mai 2024, le gouvernement a toutefois bloqué TikTok en Nouvelle-Calédonie pendant les émeutes. Le Conseil d’État a “annulé”,quelques mois après, cette décision le 1er avril 2025, la jugeant disproportionnée .

Plus récemment, dans le contexte des mobilisations lycéennes et des violences urbaines d’octobre 2026, cette possibilité a de nouveau été envisagée. Selon une enquête publiée par Blast le 24 octobre, le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu aurait demandé aux principaux opérateurs télécoms de se préparer à une éventuelle suspension temporaire de plusieurs plateformes. Cette mesure n’a finalement pas été appliquée.

Si ces mesures diffèrent par leur portée et leurs implications juridiques, qu’il s’agisse du blocage d’une plateforme, de la restriction de l’Internet mobile ou d’une coupure générale d’Internet, elles traduisent néanmoins une même logique visant à maîtriser les canaux de communication par lesquels les crises deviennent visibles et les mobilisations s’organisent.

Selon la coalition internationale Access Now , au moins 313 coupures ou restrictions intentionnelles d’Internet ont été recensées dans 52 pays en 2025. Ces chiffres recouvrent différentes formes de restrictions numériques, au-delà des seuls réseaux sociaux.

Read more: Suspension des réseaux sociaux au Gabon : pourquoi la mesure aggrave la crise au lieu de l'éteindre

Le piège du « solutionnisme sécuritaire numérique »

Pour éclairer cette logique, on peut mobiliser la critique du solutionnisme technologique développée par le chercheur Evgeny Morozov : la tendance à reformuler des situations sociales et politiques complexes en problèmes susceptibles d’être résolus par une solution technique.

Appliquée ici aux restrictions numériques, cette approche conduit à ce que l’on pourrait appeler un solutionnisme sécuritaire numérique, puisque cette grille de lecture amène à réduire une crise sociale à un problème de circulation des contenus, comme si le blocage d’une plateforme pouvait tenir lieu de réponse aux causes du conflit.

Le raisonnement n’est pas dénué de fondement. Des contenus peuvent effectivement inciter à la violence ou en favoriser la propagation. Les autorités ont le devoir de prévenir ces risques. Mais une difficulté apparaît lorsque l’on confond l’outil qui donne de la visibilité à la contestation avec les causes de celle-ci.

Une colère liée au coût de la vie, à des décisions politiques ou à une défiance envers les institutions ne disparaît pas nécessairement lorsque Facebook ou TikTok devient inaccessible. La suspension modifie les conditions de circulation de l’information et les possibilités de coordination ; elle ne constitue pas, en elle-même, une réponse aux causes sociales et politiques de la contestation.

Un rapport de recherche publié en 2025 sur le Myanmar documente la poursuite de certaines formes d’engagement malgré les restrictions numériques. Les participants décrivent des pratiques de contournement et l’utilisation de différents canaux pour maintenir la circulation de l’information et le soutien aux mobilisations.

Read more: Les influenceurs redéfinissent les médias : leçons du Kenya, du Nigeria et de l'Afrique du Sud

Ces adaptations ne rendent toutefois pas les restrictions sans effet : la surveillance, la peur et l’autocensure limitent également la participation. L’exemple montre ainsi que la répression numérique peut reconfigurer l’engagement sans nécessairement le faire disparaître.

Des stratégies de contournement

Une autre étude publiée en 2020 montre que les restrictions sur les communications numériques ne mettent pas nécessairement fin aux protestations. En Éthiopie, en décembre 2017, les manifestations se sont poursuivies malgré le blocage des réseaux sociaux, qui touchait principalement les régions d’Amhara et d’Oromia. L'étude relève notamment un pic de manifestations pacifiques simultanées, presque toutes concentrées en Oromia, pendant la période de blocage.

Au Soudan, entre décembre 2018 et février 2019, les restrictions d’accès aux réseaux sociaux imposées sous Omar el-Béchir n’ont pas non plus empêché la poursuite des mobilisations. Ces cas illustrent la capacité des mouvements de contestation à se maintenir malgré la restriction de certains canaux de communication numériques, sans pour autant démontrer que ces mesures seraient dépourvues d’effets.

Il serait excessif d’en conclure qu’aucune restriction ne peut réduire un risque immédiat. En revanche, ces travaux invitent à ne pas assimiler la diminution de l’activité en ligne à la résolution du conflit.

D’abord, les échanges peuvent tout simplement se déplacer : réseaux privés virtuels (VPN), applications alternatives, appels téléphoniques ou rencontres physiques, lorsque ces moyens restent accessibles.

Ensuite, les restrictions privent aussi les citoyens d’informations utiles et les institutions de moyens de démentir des rumeurs ou d’observer l’activité sociale. Ce n’est pas parce qu’on éteint la lumière que la vie s’arrête . Bien au contraire, elle continue dans le noir, sans aucun moyen de surveillance.

Enfin, une coupure peut elle-même devenir un objet de contestation, notamment si sa durée et ses justifications sont peu transparentes.

L’enjeu est donc autant communicationnel que sécuritaire. Dans une crise, il est réducteur de considérer que les plateformes ne véhiculent que des messages. Elles participent à la formation des perceptions collectives, à l’interprétation des événements et à la confiance — ou à la défiance — envers les pouvoirs publics. Supprimer temporairement un espace de discussion ne supprime pas les représentations qui s’y sont construites.

Le Gabon, révélateur d’un changement de gouvernance

Le cas gabonais soulève une question supplémentaire. La réouverture des plateformes s’accompagne d’un cadre réglementaire renforcé, qui impose désormais aux utilisateurs de s’identifier formellement afin de lier leurs comptes à leur identité réelle. Les modalités concrètes de cette identification restent toutefois à préciser. Il ne s’agit donc plus seulement de décider quand suspendre les réseaux sociaux, mais aussi de redéfinir les conditions de leur utilisation.

La régulation des contenus illicites et la prévention des appels à la violence répondent à des objectifs légitimes. Elles doivent toutefois être distinguées des restrictions générales d’accès ou des dispositifs d’identification, qui soulèvent des questions de proportionnalité, de protection des données et de liberté d’expression.

La suspension des réseaux sociaux constitue-t-elle une réponse ponctuelle à une menace ou peut-elle ouvrir la voie à un contrôle durable de l’espace numérique ?

Au Gabon, la suspension des réseaux sociaux n'a pas fait disparaître les revendications sociales. En octobre 2026, des tensions persistaient, notamment dans l’ enseignement professionnel , où plusieurs mois de grève rendaient encore nécessaires des négociations avec les autorités. D'autres conflits, comme celui des Sucreries du Gabon , ont connu une accalmie grâce à l'ouverture d'une médiation.

La situation témoigne donc d'un apaisement partiel, sans résolution de l'ensemble des revendications. Si la suspension a pris fin le 24 octobre, rien ne permet d'établir à ce jour qu'elle ait contribué à réduire les tensions sociales.

Agir sur les causes, pas seulement sur les canaux

L’efficacité d’une restriction numérique ne peut se mesurer à la seule diminution des publications ou des échanges en ligne. Elle doit également s’apprécier au regard de l’évolution des tensions sociales, de la circulation d’informations fiables et du maintien de la confiance entre les citoyens et les institutions.

Au-delà de l’opposition entre sécurité et liberté d’expression, la gestion des crises invite ainsi à repenser les stratégies de communication publique, en privilégiant le dialogue, la transparence et des réponses adaptées aux causes des mobilisations. Car si les États disposent des moyens techniques pour interrompre les communications numériques, leur capacité à résoudre les crises sociales repose avant tout sur leur aptitude à en comprendre et à en traiter les causes profondes.

Faire taire les réseaux sociaux ne signifie pas nécessairement apaiser la société. Cela peut aussi traduire la tentation de recourir à une solution technique pour rendre moins visibles les problèmes sociaux à l’origine de la crise, plutôt que de chercher à les résoudre.

stories.title: Washington’s War, Beijing’s Tanks
stories.summary: China is absorbing the shock of the Iran War for the rest of Asia. The post Washington’s War, Beijing’s Tanks appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sinopec oil storage tanks in Wuhan, China (Shutterstock)

Donald Trump insists that oil is moving through the Strait of Hormuz above pre-war levels. Brent crude settled at $117.38 on Friday and was still trading near $114 on Monday, a day after Qatari mediators arrived in Tehran to head off the next round of fighting. The market heard the president and kept bidding.

It has cause. The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran is in its ninth month, and October has been its worst month yet for shipping. At least 12 ships were attacked in and around the strait in the week ending October 16, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations. Energy Secretary Chris Wright says that Gulf crude flows are back to 80-90 percent of pre-war levels; Kpler’s tracking put September’s Hormuz exports at about 44 percent of February’s. Washington and Tehran have both drawn up plans to resume the wider war, possibly after Americans vote on November 3.

The bill has not been split evenly. The International Monetary Fund now assumes that Hormuz traffic will not resume until March 2027, and it has warned that poorer economies dependent on imported oil are the most exposed. It cut its 2026 forecast for the Philippines, which draws 95 percent of its crude imports from the Middle East, to 3.4 percent from 5.6 percent in January. Fuel subsidies have widened budget deficits in Indonesia and Malaysia. Americans are paying as well: diesel has climbed about 70 percent in a year, to $6.28 a gallon .

Washington’s response has run to naval escorts, threats of more bombing, a sanctions waiver for Russian diesel, and appeals to European governments to release their own diesel stocks. Washington has also relied on China to absorb a large share of the shock.

China imported a record 11.6 million barrels a day in 2025, filling storage while crude was at its cheapest since 2020. When the strait closed, Chinese refiners stopped chasing every cargo and ran down what they had banked. Second-quarter imports fell 32 percent from the first quarter, to 8.1 million barrels a day. In September they were 21.5 percent lower than a year earlier, and onshore crude stocks fell by 57 million barrels in the month on Vortexa’s count, the largest monthly draw in analysts’ records.

Beijing’s motive was commercial. Refiners facing $100 crude and thin margins had every reason to burn stock instead of buying. The effect spread well beyond China. The U.S. Energy Information Administration found that weaker Chinese buying reduced global demand and softened the price impact of the lost supply. Société Générale ranked the pullback among the largest offsets to the shock, behind only Saudi Arabia’s rerouting and ahead of the coordinated reserve releases by the United States, Europe, and Japan.

Western strategic reserves exist to steady markets in exactly this kind of emergency. China’s tanks, filled for China’s own security, did more of that work.

The neighbors felt it most. Kpler has described China as the oil market’s main balancing mechanism, and more than half of Southeast Asia’s crude imports come from the Middle East. Every cargo Chinese refiners passed up was one fewer bid against Manila or Hanoi in the spot market.

China kept buying, just not crude. Customs data show its imports grew 22.3 percent in yuan terms in the first nine months, faster than its exports, and September imports rose 31 percent in dollar terms. Some of that is price. For suppliers across Asia, China remained a growing customer in a year when their own fuel bills were climbing.

The cushion is not bottomless. Fuel is where it has worn thinnest: Chinese diesel and gasoline inventories fell in September to their lowest in more than a decade as refiners shipped product abroad. Beijing held back October export approvals over its Golden Week holiday, then resumed fuel exports , a step Reuters said would ease tight global fuel markets. Approvals now come month by month.

Crude is less stretched than it looks. A Reuters calculation shows that China drew on stocks in four of the past five months, yet heavy buying before the war leaves it with a small surplus for the first three quarters and a stockpile of at least 1.2 billion barrels. Imports are edging up again, and Kpler expects seaborne arrivals of 8-8.5 million barrels a day this quarter. If refiners rush back to refill at $115, China stops being Asia’s cushion and becomes one more bidder.

Beijing has a second buffer it has barely used: its own households. Third-quarter growth of 4.5 percent leaned on factories. Exports jumped 36.3 percent in September, while consumer prices rose just 0.9 percent and property investment fell 20.6 percent over nine months. Europe’s deficit with China hit a record $34.8 billion in September, and Ursula von der Leyen says that the European Commission is building an instrument, due in December, that could restrict the access of some Chinese goods to the single market.

Chinese households might be able to carry more. Retail sales rose 1.1 percent in September against a forecast of 0.5 percent; excluding cars they grew 3.9 percent , the fastest since October 2025. China’s top economic planner pledged on October 20 to expand domestic demand with greater force. December’s Central Economic Work Conference will show whether that means bigger rural pensions and health coverage that follows migrant workers into the cities, or another round of infrastructure that adds to the very output Brussels is counting.

Washington’s part is simpler. No stockpile, Chinese or American, substitutes for a settlement that lets tankers through without being shot at. The IMF has penciled in a closed strait until March 2027. Every month a deal arrives before then is a month Asia stops paying for a war it did not start.

November’s customs and retail figures will show which China Asia is dealing with this winter. If crude imports stay restrained while shoppers keep accelerating, the region gets a second cushion, made of Chinese demand rather than Chinese storage. If the tanks refill first and the shoppers stall, Asia loses the first cushion without gaining the second.

The strait will reopen on terms settled between Washington and Tehran. How much of the bill Asia pays until then is still being decided in Beijing.

stories.body:
Low water levels on Lake Powell have revealed parts of Glen Canyon that were long submerged. Ted Wood

WATER

Lake Powell recently dropped to a historic low, slashing hydropower and the flow of water downstream. As drought deepens, groups are pushing to drain the lake entirely to reveal its long-submerged rock arches and spires and allow wildlife along the Colorado River to recover.

By Jim Robbins • October 29, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

The 27-year-long drought in the Southwestern U.S. — the longest dry period in the last 1,200 years — is taking a serious toll on the flow of the Colorado River. Climate change is shrinking the snowpack in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains, the source of roughly 80 percent of the river’s annual flow, and higher temperatures are melting the snowpack earlier in the year, which saps runoff in late summer and fall. Warmer weather is also increasing evaporation from the river’s 40 reservoirs, including its two largest — Lakes Powell and Mead.

Last month, Lake Powell, on the Utah-Arizona border, reached a record low, at less than 150 feet above dead pool, the point at which water can no longer flow through the Glen Canyon Dam’s bypass tubes to reach Lake Mead, behind Hoover Dam, 300 miles downstream. The low water levels reduced the generation of hydropower from both reservoirs, complicated how riverine ecosystems are managed, and slashed deliveries of water to the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California, and Nevada.

Farmers are fallowing fields. Developers in some areas have paused housing construction for lack of guaranteed water supplies. And the Bureau of Reclamation has curtailed its “environmental flows” — releases of cold water from Powell — which is threatening protected fish and preventing the buildup of sandbars that provide habitat for wildlife in the Grand Canyon. No matter how the river is managed going forward, observers say, ecosystems both downstream and up will see significant changes.

Faced with the prospect of even lower Colorado River levels, the federal and state governments have been scrambling to come up with ways to meet the competing demands of disparate interests that rely on its flow, from topping off Lake Powell with water diverted from upstream reservoirs, to slashing downstream water deliveries by 40 percent, to paying farmers to keep their allocations of water in the river. The crisis is even causing some to consider a fix once deemed unthinkable: draining Lake Powell entirely.

A map of Lake Mead and Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Yale Environment 360 / Created with Datawrapper

When the Glen Canyon Dam was built in the 1960s, proponents hyped its benefits: cheap hydropower, subsidized water for cotton and alfalfa growers, real estate on the new lakeshore, and a playground for boaters. But detractors bemoaned the drowning of Glen Canyon itself, a red rock labyrinth of gorges, spires, cliffs, and grottoes that conservationists described as even more beautiful than the Grand Canyon.

Over the decades, some environmental advocates have argued for removing the Glen Canyon Dam and restoring the canyon, but the idea was always dismissed as too expensive and, because it would wipe out power generation, wildly impractical.

Now, a more tempered approach is gaining support, with groups like the Glen Canyon Institute arguing not to remove the dam but to drain Lake Powell through new diversion tunnels that would be drilled below the existing bypass tubes, close to the riverbed. The upsides, say advocates, would be manifold. The water would boost hydropower production in Lake Mead. The stunning formations of Glen Canyon and sites sacred to Indigenous people would reemerge. Wildlife would return, and riparian habitat above and below the dam site would eventually be restored. The plan is called Fill Mead First.

For more than four decades, the Glen Canyon Dam was considered a huge asset to the river basin, said Eric Balken, executive director of the Glen Canyon Institute. But it’s now “becoming a liability because it might actually prevent water from flowing downstream. All of the core assumptions around the dam have been turned on their head.”

The Glen Canyon Dam. George Frey / Getty Images

That’s because of the dam’s structural limitations. If the lake drops below minimum power pool, its penstocks — the large pipes that send water to the dam’s eight turbines — will be left stranded, high and dry. Lake water will instead be released through bypass tubes, which sit below the penstocks but have less than half their capacity to discharge water.

These tubes were not built for sustained long-term use, and sending high volumes of water through them could cause vibrations, scouring, and other effects that could cause irreparable damage to the dam. While the Bureau of Reclamation has long warned about relying solely on the bypass tubes to release water, after inspecting and relining them in 2025 it said they might work if needed. But another challenge will remain: Relying on the narrow tubes will make it harder for Upper Basin states (Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) to meet their delivery obligations to Lower Basin states and, by international agreement, Mexico.

Allowing more water to flow through the Glen Canyon Dam — by draining the lake through the existing bypass tubes and newly drilled diversion tunnels near the riverbed — is no longer dismissed out of hand. “That conversation has evolved,” said Kathryn Sorensen, director of research at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University.

A diagram of the Glen Canyon Dam. The minimum power pool is the lowest level at which it is possible to generate power. Dead pool is the point at which water stops flowing through the dam. Yale Environment 360

Lower release structures, said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University, are “an utterly reasonable idea” and should be part of the discussion. As for Powell’s potential loss of hydropower, proponents of dam removal say those megawatts could be replaced with solar power. The new Gemini solar plant near Las Vegas has a capacity of 690 megawatts; the Glen Canyon Dam currently has a capacity of around 730 megawatts.

The Lower Basin states, which primarily take their water from Lake Mead and are seeing their allotments held back to prop up Lake Powell, have urged the federal government to consider modifying the dam with lower outlets rather than cutting back on deliveries, as the Biden administration ordered in 2024.

“Addressing the infrastructure limitations may be the one long-term measure that would best achieve operation and management improvements to the Glen Canyon Dam,” representatives of the Lower Basin states wrote to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum last year.

Draining Lake Powell completely “could [annually] reduce evaporative losses by a couple hundred thousand acre-feet,” said Sorensen: Experts say 11 percent of the water in the reservoir is lost to evaporation each year. “On a river that is much smaller than anyone expected, that water really matters,” she said. But while the Glen Canyon Institute plan is gaining some traction, she added, “it faces a lot of obstacles.”

Boaters travel under Gregory Natural Bridge, in Lake Powell, which was under water until 2021. Francisco Kjolseth / The Salt Lake Tribune

One of those obstacles is the federal government, which did not even consider the possibility of draining Lake Powell as an option in its recent environmental impact statement — finalized in August — which addressed ways to manage the Colorado over the next 10 years.

Officials in Page, Arizona, which has a thriving water-based recreation industry, have also opposed draining the lake. The BlueRibbon Coalition, which represents off-road and motorized outdoor recreation, leads the opposition. It has put forward a model bill called the Colorado River Abundance Act, which would supply treated water to Lower Basin states, allowing more water to be retained in Lake Powell. The treated water would come from nuclear-powered desalination of seawater and briny water and through “advanced water reuse,” in which wastewater is cleaned with filter technologies, at an estimated cost of $40 billion.

Another obstacle is time: New diversion tunnels would likely take a decade to study, design, and build. And the price tag could be in the billions.

The Colorado’s reduced flows are, meanwhile, taking a toll on riverine ecosystems, which scientists call “novel” because they have been radically altered by 70 years of human activity — most significantly by the elimination of seasonal flooding. For a number of reasons, including low lake levels, the Bureau of Reclamation has canceled many environmental flows from the Glen Canyon Dam in recent years, depriving the Colorado of a large pulse of sediment, which is a part of the river’s natural ecology. The flows rebuild sandbars and beaches used by boaters in the Grand Canyon, and they create shallow-water habitat for threatened and endangered native fish.

Long-drowned cottonwood trees in Lake Powell have resurfaced as water levels have dropped. Carolyn Cole / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

The Bureau also occasionally releases cold water from the dam to lower the river’s temperature and keep invasive, warm-water-loving bass from taking up residence in the Grand Canyon stretch and displacing native fish. But because of the drought, which is already reducing hydroelectric production, those releases have also been curtailed.

Draining the lake completely would allow Glen Canyon to recover as the river flushes out built-up sediment, experts say. Native cottonwoods and willows would take root and help push out invasives, like tamarisk. River otters, beavers, birds, and amphibians would return to the canyon. And the drowned red rock arches, natural bridges, amphitheaters, and waterfalls would gradually emerge from the muck, along with thousands of sites sacred to Native Americans.

A shift in the hydrological regime would also have profound effects on hundreds of miles of river ecosystems below Glen Canyon Dam, including in the Grand Canyon. “It would change in ways that are only partially predictable,” said Schmidt. “Suddenly the river would have great fluctuations. The river would have much more sediment. The river would be much more turbid.” A refugium of native fish, the Grand Canyon would suddenly be swamped with non-native fish, many of which were introduced into Lake Powell for sport fishing. “It just keeps getting more complicated,” Schmidt acknowledges. “It’s all a trade-off in this screwy manmade world.”

For now, Fill Mead First remains a pipe dream, one that’s getting a lot more attention as river levels continue to drop and global temperatures rise. The federal government will ultimately decide the Glen Canyon Dam’s future, but Eric Balken, for one, thinks a new regime is long overdue. Propping up Lake Powell is “kicking the can down the road,” he said. “But they are running out of road.”
