stories.title: FBI working with Binance after crypto exchange hit by $6.3bn heist – business live
stories.summary: Blockchain intelligence firm TRM says North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking unit is responsible for the largest crypto theft on record Explainer: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe? Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack? North Korean group blamed for $6.3bn Binance hack in biggest ever crypto heist Most major cryptocurrencies have fallen in value since news of the Binance theft broke, Coinmarketcap data shows . That includes: Bitcoin : -2.35% over the last 24 hours, to $77,940 Ethereum : -3.6%, to $2,227 BNB : -5.6%, to $706 Solana : -2.67%, to $97 Chainlink : -3.1%, to $11.02 Temporarily suspended withdrawals while we complete a security revamp of the withdrawal service and its related addresses Revoked the affected address authorizations Engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds Our team hasn’t stopped. We’re working closely with law enforcement to ensure the matter is handled appropriately - and I’ll share what I can, as soon as I can. Continue reading...
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Chainalysis: Hackers using 'never-seen-before laundering patterns'

US blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis has spotted that the hackers behind the Binance theft are using “ never-seen-before” patterns to launder the stolen assets and stay ahead of the authorities.

They report that thousands of transactions have taken place in a short period, suggesting the attackers are using automation to obscure the trail of funds.

Rather than simply moving funds onward, they repeatedly circulate them among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses involved earlier in the sequence.

Chainalysis explains :

double quotation mark While billions of dollars in crypto under their control were denominated in unfreezable cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, billions more were held in stablecoins like USDT and USDC that can be frozen. It was only a matter of time before the issuers of those stablecoins would freeze those funds — in coordination with law enforcement and industry partners such as Chainalysis. Freezing funds takes time. The attacker attempted to stay ahead of that process by quickly moving $500 million of stablecoins into a wallet whose job it was to swap out those freezable assets to non-freezable assets. Over nearly 20 minutes it swapped $325 million in stablecoins into $285 million in ETH. Ten minutes later, the exploiter sent the remaining $175 million in stablecoins to stopover wallets, likely trying to move faster than a blacklist or freeze. But the industry caught up with them more quickly than they expected: by 5:14 pm eastern the freezes started.

Binance: We're conducting a full security review

Richard Teng adds that Binance is rebuilding its withdrawal service.

It will not be switched back on until it passes “rigorous testing”, he says, but adds that he’s “very hopeful” that users will be able to withdraw funds prior to the Sunday deadline.

Binance is also conducting a full security review, he continues.

And, the company intends to publish a proof of reserves report by Monday.

Binance: This was a complex attack

Richard Teng then confirms, in his video message, that the hack appears to have involve a compromised laptop – as reported a few hours ago.

However, he then reveals that Binance’s investigation has also uncovered “additional points of breach”.

Teng says

double quotation mark This was a complex attack. The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they want, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate.

Binance's Teng: We're working 'hand in hand' with global law enforcement

Binance has released a new video message from co-CEO Richard Teng.

Teng starts by thanking Binance’s users for their “patience and understanding”, as well as partners who froze assets stolen in the hack.

Teng says Binance is working “hand in hand” with global law enforcement “to seek justice”.

He says:

double quotation mark Rest assured that we are working non-stop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust. I want to be clear, we are committed to covering all hacked losses through our company funds. Your assets are safe.

The good news is that Binance is recoving stolen assets for users, Teng adds.

He also explains that the hack hit Binance’s own ‘hot wallet’.

The “vast majority” of customer funds are held in ‘cold wallets’ and are moved to a hot one when a user makes a withdrawal, he explains.

[A hot wallet is one that is connected to the internet, while cold wallets remain offline where they should be protected from online hackers.]

FBI: We're engaged with partners over Binance hack

The FBI has now confirmed it is looking into the Binance security breach.

The FBI said in a statement, via Reuters , that it was “aware of the incident and ‌is engaged with relevant public and private partners to ​understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate ⁠investigative steps”.

Strategy chair (and bitcoin zealot) Michael Saylor says Binance needs to deliver on its promise to compensate customers affected by the hack

Posting on X (as his company’s share price drops around 10%), Saylor explains:

double quotation mark Binance has committed its own balance sheet to making customers whole. I expect it to deliver. Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security, and emerge stronger and more resilient.

As Strategy owns around 848,000 bitcoin, it needs this to happen!

Earlier today the cofounder and former CEO of Binance asked Elon Musk not to “troll” the company, and instead “show some support”.

Changpeng Zhao appeared to be riled by Musk posting several emojis in response to posts on X about the hack.

That included a grimace in reply to a post reminding peopl that collapsed crypto exchange FTX had, like Binance today, said it had enough funds to cover clients’ holdings.

In response, CZ reminded Musk that Binance owns a stake in his SpaceX business:

double quotation mark Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop. Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!

Binance’s chief customer service officer Yi He weighed in too, saying:

double quotation mark Reporting to the major shareholder: Our company’s revenue for the year is sufficient to cover the losses, so we do not yet need to sell the SpaceX shares you are bullish on.

The tech-focused Nasdaq is also suffering early losses: it’s down 2.5%.

Chip stocks are leading the sell-off, after Intel startled Wall Street last night with surprisingly weak financial forecasts.

Shares in Intel , which warned of a “slowdown” in the PC market, have plunged by almost 29% in early trading, with rival AMD (-9.3%) and chip designed ARM (-9.9%) close behind.

Shares in companies exposed to the crypto world are dropping sharply at the start of trading in New York.

Coinbase , the US crypto exchange, are down 11.5% at the start of trading.

Strategy , which pioneered the idea of being a Bitcoin treasury company are down 10%.

Explainer: The Binance hack

You’ve probably got a lot of questions about the mult-billion dollar theft of crypto assets at Binance – and we have some answers!

Here’s our explainer on what could be the biggest theft of any kind in history:

The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors.

Farrell said ( via CNBC ):

double quotation mark “The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance.”

There’s a risk that bitcoin drops to levels hit in the summer, warns David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation.

double quotation mark Bitcoin sliced through support at $80,000 overnight as news came through of a security breach at Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange. Binance estimates that the incident could involve as much as $6.3 billion. It has frozen around $3 billion in cryptocurrency so far, and has promised to cover all losses. There is speculation that the hack originated in North Korea. This is a tough one for cryptos. Bitcoin had done a solid job in holding on to support around $80,000 over the past six weeks. But the break was conclusive, as bitcoin closed in on $76,000. The next big level of support is $75,000. But a break below here would open up the possibility of a retest of summer lows.

Back in July, Bitcoin slipped as low as $60,000, just half its all-time high, as this chart of the year’s action shows:

FBI and US Secret Service 'working with Binance' after $6.3 billion hack

Binance ⁠is working with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, ​including the Federal Bureau ⁠of Investigation (FBI) and the United ⁠States Secret Service (USSS), after ​hackers ‌stole ‌a record $6.3bn from the platform, a person familiar with the situation told ‌Reuters.

Bitcoin is dipping lower – it’s now down 1.85% today at $77,374, adding to last night’s 3% drop.

That might indicate some nervousness about holding crypto assets…

...except some non-crypto assets are also weaker today. Spot silver, for example, is down 4% and just dropped below the $50/oz level for the first time since November 2025.

The Binance hack shows the perils of accidentally clicking on a rogue link, argues Suzy Pallett, president of international cybersecurity conference Black Hat ,

double quotation mark “The Binance incident looks set to become the biggest crypto heist in history, and what’s striking is how familiar this playbook is. Billions can vanish because one person clicked the wrong thing, and with cyberattacks like these, it all starts by compromising a person, not a platform. “The question now is not only who executed this attack, but how money like this gets laundered and cashed out once it’s been stolen. It’s a complicated process, and if we really want to understand how hackers execute attacks like these, we need to be working closely with the people who hunt these perpetrators down. “Journalists, law enforcement, and the cybersecurity industry have a wealth of intelligence to offer when it comes to large-scale financial attacks, and with international collaboration between these communities, we can collectively work faster and more efficiently to protect against these common exploits.”

[as covered earlier, the hack appears to have been perpetrated through a “compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop”, though Binance insist it was a more complex attack process than just a single click…]

Hit by the Binance hack? Let us know!

Alexander Shirtcliff , head of commercial disputes and class actions at legal firm Edwin Coe , suggests Binance customers might need to consider legal action to recover losses:

Although Binance insists it has “publicly committed to cover losses”, Edwin Coe suggests “blandishments” from the board of Binance are largely for press consumption.

Shirtcliff says:

double quotation mark Taking the current standard user terms at face value, they contain limits to Binance’s liability to customers and I see no commitment on using the Secure Asset Fund. Neither will it be quick. How Binance decides to distribute the funds, to whom and when, the value of Bitcoin being volatile, will create a constellation of additional legal issues for the exchange which it will take time to work through. “It is very unlikely that voluntarily distributed reserves will be enough and customers will have to seek to compel Binance to make them whole. That will mean litigation. A collective action is sometimes the only way for some in cases like this to seek recourse, pooling resources to make litigation viable for many individual victims.”

Shirtcliff also suggests there could be litigation concerning who owns the assets which have been frozen since the hack was discovered.

Binance promises to 'weather this storm' as asset recovery begins

Binance has announced that it has “begun recovering affected assets for users” lost in the heist.

It says it is working with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.

Binance explains that it will use its own reserves of crypto assets to cover losses where possible, and buy other assets in the market:

double quotation mark Binance has already reserved over $6.34B of company funds to cover this incident. $5B of these funds are already held in the exact token assets that were impacted. We are completing the purchase of the remaining amount by buying token assets through market channels and OTC channels. We are doing this to match the format of the remaining token assets and address any asset shortfalls. This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity and OTC settlement also takes time. We will share more progress as soon as we can. These figures do not include frozen or protected assets, which remain subject to ongoing recovery and verification. Currently, $3bn has been frozen, with thanks to our industry partners. We are working with partners and law enforcement to recover the frozen assets.We will continue to use company resources to cover confirmed shortfall and will provide further verified updates as recovery efforts progress. Ultimately, all user funds will be verified publicly through our Proof of Reserves. We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.

stories.body:
Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loom

The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.

Estimates ranged from ⁠a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.

The growth comes as resilient consumer spending and AI -driven ⁠business investment has more than ⁠offset the impact ​of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East .

The change is in stark contrast to ​households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in ‌ Donald Trump ’s record-low approval ratings ‌and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of about 2%. New data from the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, showed that prices increased 0.5% for the month in September and the annualized inflation rate rose to 3.6%. In August, the PCE’s inflation rate was 3.4%.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to an annualized 3.1%.

The consumer price index , a separate measure of inflation released by the Department of Labor that was released earlier in October, had also shown inflation rising in September, with the annualized inflation rate going from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September.

Despite the rise in prices, the US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.

Increasing interest rates can slow inflation, at the risk of slackening economic activity and the jobs market. Because inflation is still hot, economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding ‌at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”

Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the ​strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect ⁠this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.

Consumer spending, ​which accounts for more ​than two-thirds of the economy, increased at ​a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in ​the second quarter. Historically low ‌layoffs and moderate ​hiring are helping ​to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged behind inflation.

But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon – about $1 a gallon more than a year ago – as the US-Israel war on Iran drags on, economists anticipate a slowdown in consumer spending.

Multiple polls have shown Donald Trump’s approval rating on the economy have plummeted in the weeks before the election, with voters citing frustration over rising gas and grocery prices. Overall consumer sentiment , measured by the University of Michigan is down 15% from February, before the start of the war with Iran, as consumers expect more inflation to come.

Thinktank says chancellor has given himself a mountain to climb after ducking big decisions in low-key speech

John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget failed to cover a £28bn shortfall in the public finances needed to avoid a return to austerity, according to Britain’s leading tax and spending experts.

A day after his address to the Commons , the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the chancellor had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking several big decisions in his debut tax and spending statement.

After his low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, the thinktank said Healey had left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms.

But as the war in the Middle East fuels a surge in inflation – raising the cost of delivering public services – the chancellor has in effect pencilled in large cuts in the run-up to the next general election.

Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

“It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review,” she said.

With Labour having promised there would be no return to austerity, and as Andy Burnham’s government prepares for the next election, she said it appeared extremely unlikely that Healey would follow through with such cuts.

“A clear short-term risk with the chancellor’s choices is that next year – with low headroom and a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments – we see another season of damaging speculation about tax rises,” she said.

In his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock emanating from the Middle East war.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – allowing a hit to the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drives up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

after newsletter promotion

Faced with grim forecasts for household living standards and growth in the British economy, the IFS said it was a “reasonable choice” for the chancellor to allow for a modest reduction in headroom.

However, his deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the thinktank to criticise his plans for meeting the fiscal rules, because they in effect relied on him cutting public spending or announcing tax increases that he had yet to prepare the public for.

“My concern is not that it would be impossible to deliver the implied cuts to other services – that could be done. But I’m sceptical that this government would be willing to do it,” Miller said.

Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’

The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.

Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.

In the second season of the popular spy thriller, produced by the Japanese TBS network, Masato Sakai plays a salaryman who is drawn into a web of international crime and espionage.

The backlash began this week when Chinese state media blasted the portrayal of Chinese agents using “ruthless violence” to torture members of a secret unit of Japan ’s self-defence forces, calling it a “deliberate smear” against Beijing.

Chinese media said that some of the torture methods were similar to those Japanese troops used against Chinese civilians during the second world war.

The state-run tabloid Global Times said the acts shown in the episode “bear striking similarities to the torture inflicted on Chinese nationals by invading Japanese troops” during the war, adding that the drama “distorts the truth by attributing these atrocities to modern Chinese characters”.

In the 4 October episode, a Chinese agent is seen cutting off the fingers of the Japanese intelligence officer and stabbing him in the abdomen.

Sanrio said in a statement: “Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people.

“We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects.”

The drama’s first season, set in a fictional central Asian country, avoided controversy, but its latest season is being shown at a time of increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Tokyo.

Japan’s conservative prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, set off a diplomatic row in November last year when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan.

Takaichi said earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and hoped to watch them over the year-end and new year holidays.

China is a crucial overseas market for Sanrio, whose cast of characters includes My Melody and Cinnamoroll – both featured in Vivant-themed merchandise.

The Tokyo-based company racked up 781m yuan ($117m) in revenue from the Chinese market in the first half of this year, according to Chinese media, up more than 40% from the same period last year.

The backlash against Sanrio comes days after the French international footballer Kylian Mbappé was dropped by several Chinese brands after he jokingly referred to Mao Zedong as a “dictator”. The Real Madrid forward, who is nicknamed the “dictator” for his influence on the game, later apologised for his “ill-judged” remarks.

stories.body:
The chancellor outlined ‘the biggest wave of devolution in a generation’ – but large swathes of the country are excluded

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

In just two years, there could be dozens of mayors preparing to spend billions of pounds as part of Andy Burnham’s mission to devolve greater powers across England.

Fresh devolution deals could also be in place following negotiations with leaders in Scotland, Wales and possibly Northern Ireland, allowing the prime minister to say at the next election that he has fulfilled a promise to rewire Britain’s political landscape with a view to giving more local control.

This was the message from John Healey’s first budget , which outlined the direction of travel and put in some milestones, including a 2028 commitment to devolve some income tax receipts to mayors of strategic authorities (MSAs). He added the commitment that next year, 20% of business rates revenues will go to mayors.

He told MPs that he was offering mayors 100% of their business rates income by the end of the decade and the ability to tax visitors who stay in hotels and B&Bs in their aream, via a new overnight visitors levy.

It would mean, Healey said: “New powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics. The biggest wave of devolution in a generation, driving good growth in every postcode delivered to the British people by this Labour government.”

However, Burnham’s signature phrase that he will bring “good growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” will face scrutiny once it becomes clear large parts of the country are excluded.

Manchester, the West Midlands and Liverpool City region head a list of 14 areas already governed by a mayor.

Healey said the 14 were on course to get enhanced deals, while ministers were in the final stages of signing 10 more agreements, creating MSAs for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay; Hertfordshire; Lancashire; Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland; Stoke and Staffordshire; Surrey; Thames Valley (Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Swindon); and Wessex.

Last month, Essex county council leaders agreed to adopt an MSA to secure about £1.2bn of funding over 10 years. Cornwall’s leaders, who secured a special devo deal under the previous Tory government, were at No 10 North last week – the hub of devolution discussions – hammering out an enhanced set of powers matched by extra money.

Yet there is concern that while these areas might come on board before next year, many others will be left out.

Jonathan Carr-West, chief executive of the Local Government Information Unit, a thinktank, said: “A rewired state needs every tier of government to play its part, and it needs every tier of government to be financially resilient.”

In his view, those areas without a mayor, or without a special devo deal like Cornwall, will begin to fall behind the rest, exacerbating regional inequality.

Next month, No 10 is due to publish the much-anticipated Rewiring the State delivery plan, which Burnham has said will contain the thrust of what he wants to achieve as prime minister.

Carr-West said the holes in Healey’s speech will need to be filled in by Burnham if there is to be some clarity about the way forward. “Today’s budget statement puts more, rather than less, pressure on that document,” he said.

One of the major barriers to progress is likely to be the stalled reorganisation of local government in England, which was due to convert county and district councils into a web of unitary authorities. Angela Rayner, the secretary of state for housing, local government and communities, suspended the plan in September.

Unitary authorities will carry out all the roles previously divided between counties and districts, from providing social services and education to overseeing parking and local business licences.

Several county councils have used judicial reviews to challenge the plans, forcing Rayner to rethink.

Kent is an example of an authority that is a long way from having an MSA, after the Reform UK-run county council objected to a government plan for a split into four unitaries. It has gone to court saying Kent should remain as a single entity, much like Cornwall.

Vince Maple, head of Medway council in Kent, accepts the dispute is a barrier to a deal at the moment, but says it was clear from Healey’s speech that local government reorganisation (LGR) will go ahead in some form and devo deals will follow.

“Government has made itself clear that LGR is going ahead. Most people accept it will happen,” he said.

Maple also heads the Key Cities Group of second-tier urban areas, which includes Gloucester, Sunderland and Salford. He said the expansion of MSAs to include a further 10 areas meant the government was getting closer to its “every postcode” target.

“Our members will be part of the conversation now in a way that they weren’t 24 hours ago,” he said.

There is also scepticism that the economic growth Burnham hopes to achieve from devolution may be slow to materialise.

In a judgment on the budget, the consultancy Oxford Economics , said: “A combination of limited detail, unaddressed challenges, and the length of time for any upside to show means that the devolution announcements will not lead us to revising our regional forecasts.”

Burnham will hope that rearranging the structure of local government will be enough at the next election to convince voters that change is beneficial, even if he cannot show a boost to economic growth.

stories.title: DUP blocks Michelle O'Neill's engagements over Drumcree
stories.summary: The DUP leader Gavin Robinson also confirms that Emma Little-Pengelly will not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Michelle O'Neill described the move as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented"

Published 29 October 2026

Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has been blocked by the DUP from attending an economic summit involving Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The Sinn Féin vice-president and Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly were both invited to attend the National Economic Council in Glasgow on Friday with other devolved leaders.

The DUP leader Gavin Robinson confirmed that his party colleague Little-Pengelly will not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill and permission will not be granted for the first minister to operate on a solo basis.

The move follows unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests which prevented a contentious Orange Order march in Portadown from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road .

Robinson was flanked by DUP assembly members as he spoke in the Great Hall at Parliament Buildings

A meeting of the party's ruling officer committee was held earlier on Thursday.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said the first minister's "arrogance will have consequences", but O'Neill accused the party of being "reckless and irresponsible".

"Her complaints today that she's frustrated from engaging with the British Prime Minister within the sovereign United Kingdom will so be it because her law breaking must have consequences," Robinson said.

O'Neill said the DUP leader's comments were "arrogant and supremacist" adding that the DUP "is consumed with their own internal leadership troubles and divisions".

She said she would be at the Assembly on Monday with her party colleagues to "keep showing up every day for people".

Earlier she described the move to block the meeting with the prime minister as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented".

"This is a reactive stunt, driven by the DUP's own internal pressures and electoral problems," she said in a statement posted online.

The prime minister revived the National Economic Council over the summer to encourage greater collaboration between the nations and regions.

Earlier Little-Pengelly said the concerns arising from O'Neill's conduct and the "anger and hurt felt by many people across Northern Ireland, cannot simply be ignored or minimised".

She said the decision comes after stopping a separate planned engagement with the President of Ireland, Catherine Connolly.

"I have requested a separate meeting with the Prime Minister to ensure Northern Ireland's interests, including the urgent budgetary and funding challenges facing the Executive, continue to be represented directly," she added.

The Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said it was "deeply frustrating" that the Northern Ireland executive would not be represented at the National Economic Council.

"I understand feelings are running high but it must be in the interests of the people of Northern Ireland that everyone gets round the table."

The DUP ruling committee met to discuss what steps it would take against Sinn Féin over the Drumcree dispute

O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating last month's unnotified demonstrations in Portadown , with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

The Sinn Féin deputy leader has defended her involvement, saying it was the "right thing to do".

The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said "the DUP's sham response today was beyond pathetic" adding "the DUP is interested only in clinging to office, not principle".

Alliance leader Naomi Long said refusing to attend or preventing others from attending the meeting with the prime minister was reckless and put party interests ahead of Northern Ireland's economic future and the needs of the public.

The Ulster Unionist Party leader Jon Burrows told BBC's Evening Extra programme the situation was a "political fudge" that was "all choreography and no consequences," adding that the move would "probably galvanise Sinn Féin further at the ballot box."

The Social Democratic and Labour Party's (SDLP) Matthew O'Toole said "plunging this place into more political chaos is not a sensible strategic move for unionism".

"Ultimately it's only going to make reasonable people here conclude that the largest unionist party simply doesn't want to make the status quo work," he added.

The DUP has been under pressure from unionist rivals and some within its own ranks over how to respond to the row over Drumcree.

Last week, DUP MP Carla Lockhart stepped down from the party's officer board over their leader Gavin Robinson not withdrawing Little-Pengelly to force O'Neill from their joint Stormont office.

On Thursday Lockhart said she will follow her "own course" if the party does not seek to remove Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill as Stormont's first minister.

Robinson said that while O'Neill and her party colleagues "should be punished, that does not include punishing the rest of Northern Ireland".

The Upper Bann MP, who last week quit the DUP's ruling officer board in opposition to party leader Gavin Robinson's approach, outlined her position in a letter to colleagues which she later posted on Facebook.

Other DUP representatives including assembly member Diane Forsythe have since backed Lockhart's calls for O'Neill to be "removed from office" .

On Tuesday, Forsythe said that in the absence of such "meaningful action", official engagements through the joint Executive Office should be stopped immediately as a "bare minimum".

On Wednesday, a second DUP assembly member called for O'Neill to go.

Maurice Bradley said removing O'Neill "would not, in itself, require the Assembly to collapse".

Carla Lockhart stepped down from the DUP's officer board last week

Bradley added that the party "must stand together" and "support Carla Lockhart".

Other party members including former MP Lord McCrea and Mid Ulster councillor Clement Cuthbertson have also backed Lockhart.

Party leader Robinson said last week that he was "sorry" to see Lockhart quit the DUP's officer board but added that she remained "a key part of our team".

Speaking on the BBC's The View programme , Robinson said the party had reached a democratic decision on how to deal with the Drumcree fallout.

He questioned whether it was necessary to "punish everyone in Northern Ireland when actually we should be punishing those who broke the law".

"We have considered all options and we keep all options on the table," he added.

Last week, a court heard Police Service of Northern Ireland intelligence information that dissidents may have mounted gun attacks on police had officers cleared a path for the parade.

Tony Vaughan (pictured) has shown remorse, according to a report

Published 29 October 2026

A Labour MP has said sorry in the House of Commons following complaints over his behaviour towards a female member of staff.

It comes as the Independent Expert Panel published a report , external requiring Tony Vaughan to apologise for breaching Parliament's bullying and harassment policy.

The MP for Folkestone and Hythe was found by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards to have committed the breach after a constituency staff member complained he "behaved towards [her] in an overbearing and belittling manner".

Vaughan said on Thursday he accepted the findings in full.

"As a result of these behaviours, my former colleague was upset and humiliated," he said.

"My behaviour had a real and continuing impact on her and her family, and I am truly sorry for this."

The Labour Party said it "expects the highest standards of conduct from all our members and elected representatives.

"We have robust processes in place to ensure those high standards are upheld.

"It is right that Tony Vaughan has apologised following this independent process," a spokesperson added.

'Abuse of power'

Vaughan, who has represented his Kent constituency since 2024, was found to have hugged the complainant without consent at an office event.

He also took her personal mobile phone from her hand to join an online meeting without asking permission and failed to explain why phone calls between them had ended abruptly.

Vaughan appealed the Commissioner's findings, though the Independent Expert Panel confirmed the majority of them, according to Parliament.

The sub-panel stressed that "oppressive and bullying behaviour towards [MPs'] staff members is wholly unacceptable".

It added that Vaughan's actions were breaches of "basic boundaries and courtesy" - rather than failures in management - and an "abuse of his power".

Watch: MP apologises over bullying and harassment

The politician told MPs on Thursday that he was not "sufficiently alert" to the power imbalances between him and his employee.

He added he recognised his behaviour could well impact on "someone who is vulnerable whether or not that is known".

"I made mistakes," Vaughan continued.

The 36-page report said it took account of the impact of what happened on the complainant, who has a right to anonymity.

She said she was left feeling stressed, exhausted and offended, it adds.

The report also stated that Vaughan had "expressed genuine and thoughtful remorse".

He should be required to make an "unreserved apology" to the complainant and the House by way of a personal statement in the House of Commons Chamber, it continued.

"We consider that this achieves the appropriate balance and clear messaging required regarding the behaviour expected of MPs," the report said.

Published 29 October 2026

A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.

The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.

Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.

The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".

The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."

Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.

However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph , external .

The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.

Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.

In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.

"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.

"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."

Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."

Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."

Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage

The issue has only now emerged, nearly six months after the alleged incident, because Farage was pressed on why he had not been in the House of Commons chamber for the Budget on Wednesday.

In response he said: "At the State Opening of Parliament, I got involved… I didn't want to… but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber.

"I didn't make a fuss about it, I didn't complain, but I could see given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation.

A spokesperson for the House of Commons said that a prayer card for Farage - the way in which MPs reserve seats in the Commons - did not "display a valid date stamp" and therefore "was removed in line with the usual Chamber protocol".

stories.title: What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
stories.summary: BBC Verify examines how much the welfare system costs and the options the government could use to reduce it.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 29 October 2026

Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spoken of their desire for the benefits bill to come down, but the government has not yet laid out a timetable for any reductions.

Their political opponents have criticised them for a lack of detail on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, accusing the government of delaying difficult decisions over cuts.

Official forecasts released alongside the Budget indicate welfare spending is going to increase by £79bn in cash terms over the next few years.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers behind this thorny political issue and some of the difficult options the government have to bring down welfare costs.

How much is being spent on welfare?

The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates in its latest forecasts that the cost of the welfare system will rise , external from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032.

The OBR's figures include spending on pensioners, which accounts for just under half of the total. The majority of this cost is on the state pension.

However, if we look at the size of welfare spending relative to the size of the overall economy the OBR's projections are less dramatic, increasing from 11.1% today to 11.3% of GDP in 2032.

Total welfare spending would also remain below the peak of around 12% of GDP in 2013 following the global financial crisis, leading some economists and researchers to question the idea that welfare spending is out of control. , external

But there are some welfare costs that are rising rapidly.

Spending on health and disability related benefits, in particular Personal Independence Payments (PIP), is up sharply since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Accounting for inflation, spending on working-age disability benefits increased from £14bn in 2020 to £25bn in 2026 , external .

Inflation-adjusted welfare spending remains lower than 2013 because several other working-age benefits, such as Universal Credit and housing benefit, were cut by Conservative-led governments as part of their austerity programme from 2010 onwards , external .

So spending in some parts of the system has come down while it has risen in others - and there could be a connection.

Some researchers think the post-2010 welfare cuts to benefits might have created an incentive for people to claim sickness and disability benefits instead to protect their living standards , external , therefore shifting costs around the system rather than generating lasting savings.

The problem of Neets

Many also see a specific problem regarding the growing number of young people in the welfare system claiming benefits, including PIP.

Official figures show the number of 16 to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neets) has risen , external by around 230,000 since 2019 to just under one million.

Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is leading an official review into Neets and is expected to recommend major reforms designed to get many off benefits and into work.

His interim report in May estimated that annual PIP expenditure on 16 to 24-year-olds rose from £1.3bn in 2020 to around £3.2bn in 2025 , external . It also projected this cost would reach £6.5bn and cover 700,000 young people in five years' time.

PIP claimants can be in work, but official statistics show that only around one in five are , external .

What could cutting the benefits bill mean?

Politicians are often unclear about what they mean by reducing spending on welfare.

In March 2025, former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's government presented a plan which it said would save £5bn a year from health-related welfare spending by 2030 by tightening PIP access and reducing the value of health-related Universal Credit payments.

But official forecasts made it clear that annual spending on health-related welfare in cash terms was still set to rise after the reform , external , just not as rapidly as the path it had previously been on.

However, at the time the OBR did forecast the plans would help put overall UK welfare spending on a "slightly downward trajectory" as a share of the economy , external over the medium term, rather than remaining flat as had been previously projected.

So this type of relative reduction in anticipated welfare spending, rather than a cut in absolute cash terms, could be what the government seeks to deliver.

Looming reports may offer options

The final Milburn report is expected in the coming weeks, as well as a separate final report from disability minister Stephen Timms into the options for PIP reform.

There has been speculation that these could recommend creating a new welfare system for people under the age of 25 , external , so they are not eligible for PIP and receive lower payments than older people.

There are also suggestions Timms could propose a new PIP eligibility test to reduce access , external , although he was not specifically instructed to find savings.

Reforms along these lines could potentially make some savings to the welfare bill relative to the existing trajectory of rising spending, as well as reducing forecast welfare spending as share of GDP.

But some analysts argue that to be effective in delivering sustainable savings, such reforms are likely also to require the government to spend a lot more , external to enable young people in particular to get into and remain in work.

This was signalled by the interim Milburn report which noted that for every £1 the government spends on employment support for young people around £25 is spent on benefits , suggesting he could propose a significant increase in government spending on welfare-to-work schemes.

This means that any welfare savings could, in the near term at least, be offset by additional spending in other departments.

However, in the long term this approach could still deliver welfare savings if the employment support was effective.

stories.title: Trump ignored intel on China’s Nvidia spy to protect company’s stock, report says
stories.summary: Spy accused of exploiting Trump ties to Huang, funneling secrets to China.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Spy accused of exploiting Trump ties to Huang, funneling secrets to China.

Donald Trump apparently is so aligned with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—who has become the president’s key advisor on AI —that he ignored intelligence indicating that Huang was the target of a “Chinese spy plot,” and did so partly to protect Nvidia’s stock.

The New York Times spoke with people briefed on US intelligence agencies’ surveillance and granted them anonymity to discuss findings drawn from “classified intelligence.” According to sources, about a year ago, Trump was briefed that “Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access” to Huang. That “someone” was Alice Huang, or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen and former top executive at a Singapore cloud company called Megaspeed.

According to sources, the US had already suspected that Alice Huang—who is not related to Jensen Huang—was helping China evade export controls to gain access to high-end Nvidia chips through Megaspeed. But it alarmed investigators to discover that she may have used her role at Megaspeed to gain direct access to Jensen Huang. It’s now believed she may have leveraged that closeness to feed China intel not only on one of America’s leading AI companies, but also to influence Trump’s thinking on AI. As Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted last month ahead of Trump’s AI talks with China President Xi Jinping, “the president is completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia.”

At least partly due to fears that US action against the alleged spying could hobble Nvidia chip sales or disrupt the delicate US-China trade truce, Trump “chose not to do anything with the information,” sources said.

Soon after US scrutiny increased, Alice Huang’s name was removed from Megaspeed corporate documents. At this stage, it’s unclear “how closely she is still connected to Megaspeed,” NYT reported.

Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, DC, told NYT that the US accusations against Alice Huang are baseless. He accused the US of pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against China.

No warning to Nvidia CEO

It’s not clear which agencies were investigating Alice Huang or what triggered their suspicions, NYT reported. Sources also could not explain what information she may have shared with Beijing.

Nvidia has denied that she would have had access to any trade secrets, but it seems notable that Jensen Huang did not receive a defensive briefing that Americans sometimes get when they’re targets of foreign spying. Some senior officials think it’s unlikely that Jensen Huang would have “remained unaware” of Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence-gathering for the entire duration of their professional relationship, although Trump was told Jensen Huang had no knowledge at the time of his briefing. It seems possible that Jensen Huang got no briefing because US agencies worried that he might tip her off that “she was being watched,” the NYT reported.

Trump’s deep ties with tech leaders have been criticized throughout his administration, but Jensen Huang’s influence increasingly stands out . To critics, the political friendship appears to be largely based on growing his business in China. Since cozying up to Trump, the Nvidia CEO has gotten export controls relaxed and even struck a controversial deal giving the US a 25 percent cut of some chip sales so he could try to sell more chips in China. Sources told NYT that “some investigations and proposed trade sanctions involving China or Nvidia” have “ground to a halt within the Commerce Department” due to Jensen Huang’s influence.

No one’s sure when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, but NYT found social media photos that predated her role arranging a Megaspeed purchase of $2 billion in chips over the next year. If those chips ended up in China, the US worried they “could help adversaries like China develop new weapons, surveil dissidents, and leap ahead of the United States in AI development,” NYT reported. To US agencies, it’s particularly concerning that Megaspeed may be doing China’s bidding by supplying chips to giant data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia “that appear to remotely serve customers in China,” NYT reported earlier this month.

Sources told the NYT that US intelligence agencies conducted electronic surveillance of Alice Huang and found that “she was in contact with an American citizen.” Since agencies could not legally surveil the American citizen without a court order, they sought to unmask the citizen by showing a “need for information.”

“In this case, the unmasking process identified Mr. Huang as the US citizen,” NYT reported.

NYT probes Megaspeed offices for clues

Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer, and Nvidia has independently investigated whether Megaspeed is funneling its chips to China. That investigation concluded that there were no signs of diversion and that Megaspeed has raised no red flags as a customer, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told NYT.

Both Nvidia and Megaspeed insist that the cloud company has Singapore-based owners, but NYT visited the supposed offices and talked to anyone they could find to probe the actual business operations. Among red flags raised, NYT noted that staffers suggested “it’s not clear” what Megaspeed as a company does and confirmed that the Singapore director, James Tan, lives in China and is “never present.” (NYT’s review of corporate ownership documents showed Tan owns the shell company that owns Megaspeed.)

In that story published earlier this month, NYT detailed how Alice Huang was seemingly growing increasingly close to Jensen Huang, citing several photos of them together. That includes a photo at an event where she reportedly bragged, “I bet you guys I can get Jensen here,” and then he arrived in his trademark leather jacket to take whiskey shots.

Rizzo said that it was common for Nvidia’s CEO to attend parties with customers and partners, where he discussed “updates on the market.” One source told NYT that Jensen Huang had always planned to attend that party.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” Rizzo said. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

However, the US government has been investigating Megaspeed since 2024, and they’ve found suspicious boxes of Nvidia equipment that seem to be ready to ship out, rather than installed. Earlier this year, the Department of Justice took over the Commerce Department’s investigation, and Megaspeed remains under scrutiny even though Nvidia’s probes uncovered no evidence the company was helping China dodge export curb violations.

Aaron Bartnick, an assistant director for technology security and governance under the Biden administration, told NYT that Megaspeed raised “many red flags.” Among them are the company’s “ownership claims and possible ties to sanctioned entities, that should have made Nvidia’s executives question whether they should have permitted the company to have access to its AI chips.”

“It’s hard to see a justification for taking that risk,” Bartnick said.

stories.title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
stories.summary: Opponents have questioned the Budget's lack of detail on welfare reform, with the prime minister not outlining a timetable for any reductions.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 29 October 2026

Andy Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill "as soon as we possibly can", but was unable to guarantee this would happen before the next general election.

Opponents raised concerns over the lack of details on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, after welfare spending was forecast to increase from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2031/32.

Asked whether he would seek to reduce the bill before the next election, Burnham told reporters: "We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we're working flat out to that end."

He warned against "crude cuts" and said he wants to get people into "sustainable employment". The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare".

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published 1 day ago

The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.

Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.

These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.

The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.

Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.

He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."

Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.

"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."

'Huge bonus'

Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane said if the government could provide a plan to show "greater restraint" of the benefits bill, that would "play spectacularly well" with the financial markets.

Haldane, who has previously advised Burnham, told the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast: "If the government could get that through I think it would come with a huge bonus."

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

Reacting to government briefings and remarks on Thursday related to when a reduction in the benefits bill could take place, Badenoch said it "looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading".

She said: "Don't let anyone tell you this was a 'do no harm budget'. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they've harmed our national security."

Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.

Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.

Of the figure forecast for 2031/32, £209.8bn is on pensioners, including the state pension and winter fuel payments, while £110.7bn is on universal credit and legacy equivalents and £69.6bn is on disability benefits such as personal independence payments.

The government has already pledged to reform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030 , and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months.

stories.title: Kalshi and its co-founders face felony charges for violating Utah gambling laws
stories.summary: Charges filed as Trump admin tries to save Kalshi from Utah's total ban on gambling.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Charges filed as Trump admin tries to save Kalshi from Utah’s total ban on gambling.

The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets.

Meanwhile, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed criminal charges in a state court against Kalshi and its founders on Wednesday. The attorney general’s office provided us with court filings listing charges against KalshiEX, LLC , Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour , and Kalshi co-founder and COO Luana Lopes Lara .

The company and two co-founders each face 13 felony charges and one misdemeanor for violating gambling laws. The charges are based on sports bets offered on Kalshi between September 13 and September 24. “The state did not issue arrest warrants for Monsour and Lopes Lara. Instead, they have been issued summons to respond to the charges in Third District Court in Salt Lake County,” The Salt Lake Tribune wrote .

The Utah News Dispatch quoted a Kalshi statement vowing to fight the charges. “This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” the statement said, referring to similar charges the company beat in Arizona in May.

Utah, which prohibits gambling, filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.

“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”

Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

Trump admin claims sole authority

The CFTC “has filed a lawsuit against Utah to block the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets using state laws,” the commission said on Tuesday . “The lawsuit follows Utah’s decision to file civil enforcement actions in state court against CFTC-regulated markets and other businesses. Utah’s effort to restrict the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges obstructs Congress’s decision to federally preempt state law.”

If Utah can shut down Kalshi, that could spell trouble for Kalshi’s chief prediction-market rival, Polymarket, and for sports betting sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. DraftKings and FanDuel advertise availability in all US states via a mix of products , including prediction-market platforms in states like Utah. Both are registered with the CFTC.

The Utah attorney general’s office declined to comment today on the CFTC lawsuit. The CFTC previously filed lawsuits against Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin. The federal agency also filed briefs supporting Kalshi in appeals court cases.

“Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets,” CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said. “Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes—they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets. As I’ve said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that’s exactly what we’ll do.”

The US Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) gives the CFTC authority to regulate swaps. The key legal questions being grappled with by courts throughout the US are whether event contracts offered by prediction markets qualify as swaps, and whether the CFTC jurisdiction over swaps preempts states from applying their gambling laws.

US sues in same court where Utah beat Kalshi

The CFTC is suing Utah in the same US district court that previously ruled in Utah’s favor. Kalshi sued Utah in February in an attempt to stop the state from bringing an enforcement action against the prediction market.

In August, US District Judge Robert Shelby granted Utah’s motion for summary judgment and denied Kalshi’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Shelby wrote , “[T]he court concludes the federal law relied upon by Kalshi does not preempt Utah’s ability to enforce its anti-gambling laws.”

Shelby determined the text of US law makes it clear that state regulation is not forbidden. US law states that CFTC jurisdiction does not “supersede or limit the jurisdiction conferred on courts of the United States or any State,” and “explicitly provides for State regulation of its gaming laws in all but a few specified cases,” he wrote.

“Congress is aware that some States permit gambling while others do not, and the CEA explicitly provides for State jurisdiction,” Shelby wrote.

Most states in US want Supreme Court to rule

Kalshi is now appealing its loss to the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit but was unable to obtain an injunction preventing enforcement of the state gambling ban while that litigation continues. On September 8, Tenth Circuit judges denied Kalshi’s emergency motion for an injunction pending appeal. Utah filed its lawsuit seeking a shutdown of Kalshi about six weeks later.

The CFTC lawsuit against Utah makes arguments similar to the ones already rejected by the district court, although some other courts have ruled otherwise.

“Utah is not the first State that has attempted to invade the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction over swaps,” the CFTC lawsuit said. “Already, several federal courts—including the Third Circuit—have swiftly responded by issuing or affirming temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions barring the States from enforcing their gambling laws against CFTC-regulated exchanges that offer sports-related or other event contracts.”

The Third Circuit appeals court ruled that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. But Kalshi lost similar cases in the Sixth Circuit and Ninth Circuit in rulings that went in favor of Ohio, Tennessee, and Nevada.

Because circuit appeals courts are divided on the issue, it is likely that the Supreme Court will take up the case and determine whether states can apply their gambling laws to prediction markets. New Jersey petitioned the Supreme Court to resolve the circuit split, and 39 other states and the District of Columbia filed a brief supporting New Jersey’s petition.

This article was originally published on October 28 at 3:30 pm ET and updated on October 29 with information about the felony charges filed against Kalshi and its co-founders .

stories.title: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
stories.summary: Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 29 October 2026

Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget.

Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.

Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.

The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed.

The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.

Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.

According to the latest figures up to 30 September , external , 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.

The Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, previously said only a small number of these cases were approaching the two-year threshold.

However the PCS union, which represents civil servants, had warned there were "serious questions" over how long cases would remain unresolved.

Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says Published 12 February

Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions Published 29 January

Retired civil servants left in pension limbo Published 23 January

Rob Wassell, 58, had to wait more than two years following the death of his brother until he finally received the lump sum from his civil service pension on Tuesday.

After his case was highlighted by the BBC last week, Rob says he got a call from the pension scheme's complaints department who told him the payment was on its way.

However, because it was made after two years it was taxed at 45%, amounting to thousands of pounds.

If the payment was made after the rule change, it would not have been subject to tax.

Rob told the BBC he was pleased the government had addressed the issue in the Budget as this would mean others in his situation would not face a tax bill.

While he said he was happy to finally get his payment it was "a bitter pill to swallow" as he is now waiting for the outcome of a complaint review to find out if the tax will be reimbursed.

Rob said he was hopeful he would get the money back, adding: "I don't want to have to fight it anymore, it's been an ordeal already."

Rob Wassell was taxed on the payment from his brother's civil service pension

Pensions minister Torsten Bell confirmed the rule change in a letter to the chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee , external , Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who had raised concerns about the issue after it was highlighted by BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live programme.

Bell said the move would "make the position fairer for all grieving families and friends where there are delays in the payment of death benefits, whether in the Civil Service or any other pensions scheme".

He added: "Removing the tax deadline does not remove [a pension scheme's] wider duties to administer schemes prudently and without avoidable delay."

Under the previous rules, if someone died before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit was only tax-free if it was paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value was below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.

However, the government has now removed the two-year deadline so payments will no longer become taxable solely because they were made more than two years after a pension scheme was notified of the death.

The change applies to payments made from 28 October.

In his letter, the pensions minister said people who had already been impacted by avoidable delays and been taxed as a result could seek compensation through the pension scheme's complaints process and the Pensions Ombudsman.

Sir Geoffrey welcomed the announcement but said it does not "absolve Capita from processing and making payments to members of this scheme in a timely manner".

Fran Heathcote, general secretary of the PCS union, also welcomed the change but said "this situation should never have arisen in the first place".

She added: "Bereaved families must not pay the price for failures in the pension system.

"Capita is not off the hook, it continues to fail members and their families, which is why the scheme must be brought back in-house."

Capita has previously apologised for the impact of delays on pension scheme members and their families.

The company has said it is working to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with a particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging circumstances.

stories.title: Further delays for major council overhaul in nine of 14 proposed areas
stories.summary: Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger unitary authorities were put on hold last month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Local government minister Jim McMahon has announced plans in five areas will go ahead

Published 29 October 2026

The government has announced further delays to nine of 14 major council mergers, with only five now going ahead.

Proposals for 14 regions to undergo mergers of smaller councils to form larger unitary authorities was put on hold by Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner last month, following concerns around legal challenges.

Local Government Minister Jim McMahon has told MPs the review had found the government's decision-making to be "robust", but nine areas have now been withdrawn for further review.

Only five of the original 14 regions will be taken forward, after three more weeks of consultation. Shadow local government secretary Katie Lam condemned the latest news as "a farce".

Mergers will continue to progress in East Sussex, Gloucestershire, Oxfordshire , Warwickshire and Worcestershire .

But the government is seeking "legal clarity" in the remaining nine areas, which are: Derbyshire , Devon , Hertfordshire , Kent, Lancashire, Leicestershire , Lincolnshire , Nottinghamshire , and Staffordshire.

In a Commons statement, McMahon said the government was "withdrawing the decisions announced in July" for those nine areas.

"I want to be absolutely clear that this is not a reflection of the work underpinning those proposals," he added.

The review will now focus on the nine areas where current plans have been withdrawn for further review, as well as four areas where plans were withdrawn in September, in Essex , Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.

Two further areas, Cambridgeshire and West Sussex, are still waiting for merger plans to be agreed, totalling 15 regions where local government reorganisation plans remain undecided.

McMahon said: "We will move faster where we can, and some of the remaining areas may receive an outcome decision before others.

"I commit to coming back to the House with updates for another set of areas by Christmas, and every area will have an outcome by early next year."

Reconfirming local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries, he announced plans for elections to shadow councils, set to run for a year before taking over from old authorities, will now be held in May 2028.

Responding, Lam set out how the reorganisation had been beset by delays over the past two-and-a-half years.

"From start to finish this government's approach to local government reorganisation has been nothing short of a farce," she told MPs.

She added: "Naturally the taxpayer was left to pick up the tab for all of these delays - a bill which runs into the tens of millions of pounds."

Local Government Association chair Eamonn O'Brien called for a re-set of relations between the government and local councils across the country.

He said: "While today's announcement provides some certainty for some areas, many councils remain frustrated by the situation they have been placed in.

"All councils affected need urgent clarity on next steps and how costs already incurred will be met.

"There needs to be a reset in the relationship between government and councils on local government reorganisation, with local government fully engaged in shaping decisions from the outset."

All change for Oxfordshire and West Berkshire councils Published 22 hours ago
